1.1: 1.1 Argument. The Romans belong to a region of Italy. They had been preoccupied by false apostles, and under the name of our Lord Jesus Christ had been led into the law and the prophets. The Apostle recalls them to the true evangelical faith, writing to them from Corinth. Paul. BEDE. On the Acts of the Apostles he says that Paul came to the faith in the second year after the passion and resurrection of Christ, etc., up to according to the agreement of the apostles he set out for the teaching of the Gentiles. AUG., book On the Spirit and the Letter, ch. 7. He chose this name for no other reason, etc., up to Saul is interpreted restlessness and temptation. AMBROSE. Moreover, he is said to have done this according to the custom of the holy apostles, who, advancing in virtues, were called by a changed name, so that they might be new even in the name itself, such as Cephas and the sons of thunder. JEROME, Comm. on the Ep. to Philemon. Paul took this name from the first spoil which he brought to the Church, namely from Sergius Paulus the proconsul, whom he converted in Cyprus. A servant. Of a servant and a humble man God made an apostle and a lofty one; so you also be humble: For he that humbles himself shall be exalted (Luke 14). AUG. By putting down both, he testifies that there is one person of the God-man. One name he puts for the Jews, the other for the Gentiles. For Christ is a name known to the Jews, by which name they see designated the Son of God and hear him promised in the law, and if you preached another to them, they would not believe. But to the Gentiles, because they had not read it anywhere, he puts first the Savior, that is, Jesus. Christ, although it is not a proper name but a name of sacrament, like prophet and priest, is nevertheless rightly placed first, being known to the Jews; though these names have been given to many, it is only in figure; for this one alone is the true King and Priest. Called. Not by himself, but by God; or called, named by men by the privilege of the name. An apostle. Behold, from lowly to lofty. Set apart. From the doctrine of the scribes and Pharisees: this against the Jews; or, from the other apostles, in body and not in mind, whence: Separate me Barnabas and Paul for the work whereunto I have taken them (Acts 13). The Gospel. HAYMO. It is a good announcement, etc. Of God. Not invented by man.
1.2: 1.2 Which before its fulfillment did not come as sudden, but was promised long before. Hence in this matter the saying is true: One sows, and another reaps.
1.3: 1.3 Who was made to him. Who was made according to the flesh, by the work of the Holy Spirit, of the Virgin, that is, was born. The impiety of the heretics is met, who, understanding this chapter with dull heart, take Christ to be man only. By adding, therefore, according to the flesh, he reserved to the divinity its own dignity, in which Christ is the Word of God, through whom all things were made. AUG. Who was, etc., up to clothed, that he might appear fittingly to carnal men. THE SAME, Exposition on this epistle. Christ, therefore, is one person of a twofold substance; yet neither God nor man can be called a part of this person; otherwise the Son of God, before he took the form of a servant, was not whole, and grew when man was added to his divinity.
1.4: 1.4 Who was predestinated. AUG., Tract. 105 on John. This so great and so exalted and supreme elevation of the human nature was predestinated, that it had nothing higher to be raised to; just as, for us, the divinity itself had nothing lower to descend to than the assumed nature of man with the weakness of the flesh, even to the death of the cross. AUG., book 1 On the Predestination of the Saints, ch. 15. There is also a most brilliant light of predestination and grace in the very mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus, etc., up to that he who was to be, according to the flesh, the son of David, might be in power the Son of God. Of the dead of Jesus Christ. For his own or for his people's sake, he put the proper name in place of the pronoun, in the Hebrew manner, a form of speech very common especially in the old Scriptures, as: Moses did as the Lord commanded Moses. CHRYS. That is, we did not accomplish this by our own power, that we are apostles, for we did not obtain this dignity by our many sweats and labors, but we found grace.
1.5: 1.5 Among all nations. Not only among the Jews, with whom (because called without the law) they ought not to live under the law. For his name. For his glory, not ours, as you do.
1.6: 1.6 Called of Jesus Christ. That is, by him, namely by Jesus Christ. The genitive for the ablative, in the Greek manner.
1.7: 1.7 To the called saints. They were not called because they were holy, but were made holy because they were called; and therefore called, because beloved.
1.8: 1.8 I give thanks. To give thanks is to perceive that all things are given by God, and to praise him for it in heart, voice, and work. My God. AUG., book On Sheep. For this voice can belong only to the saints, of whom God is called, as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. For though there is one God of all by nature, yet he is said to be properly theirs by grace, who are proved by the merit of faith to be worshippers of his justice. For you all. Though for others, first for you, from whom great benefit came through Christ the mediator, through whom God gave you all good things. That your faith. AMBROSE. He rejoices with them in their good beginning, by which he shows love toward them, and exhorts them to progress. He says that he does all these things because their faith profits many.
1.9: 1.9 For God is my witness. That you have faith I attribute to the Lord. For I pray to him that it may be had; or he explains when he gives thanks, namely, in his prayers; how? without ceasing.
1.11: 1.11 For I long. That what he could not persuade by words, he might persuade, being present, by the power of miracles.
1.12: 1.12 To be comforted. Now I am desolate, as you also are: even if you do not feel it, so that we might be comforted.
1.13: 1.13 Brethren. Because born again, and some upright; see above: To the called saints.
1.14: 1.14 To the Greeks. He is silent about the Jews, because he is the teacher of the Gentiles. To the Greeks. He puts the Greeks first, because all worldly philosophy took its beginning from them. To the barbarians. He calls barbarians those who are, as it were, lawless, who are neither Hebrews, nor Greeks, nor Latins. To none is this preaching more specially owed. A debtor, because sent to all.
1.16: 1.16 For it is the power of God, etc. Because the incredible preaching is confirmed by signs, which is not the case with false preachers.
1.17: 1.17 For the justice of God. AMBROSE. It is that which freely justifies the ungodly through faith without the works of the law, etc., up to those who deny that this is the Christ whom God promised. Is revealed. AUG. He addresses the Gentiles according to their former state, etc., up to because, puffed up by themselves, they fell into idols. From faith, etc., AMBROSE. Of God promising, to the faith of man who believes him, etc., up to to the faith of things and of species. AUG. Faith is that by which are believed the things that are not seen, etc., up to to the faith of things, by which we shall obtain what has been believed. As it is written. In Habacuc, chap. 2, it is thus: But the just shall live by his faith. But this and many such testimonies which he cites seem to differ from the translation of the Hebrew truth which we now use: because sometimes he takes from the Seventy interpreters, sometimes, as speaking by the same spirit as the prophets, he takes only the sense, using his own words and his own arrangement.
1.18: 1.18 Against all ungodliness. Ungodliness is to have sinned against God, injustice against men; or the ungodly is the unbeliever like the idolater; the unjust is he who by depravity of action departs from equity. Of those men that detain the truth. As if to say: Why wrath against them for ungodliness, when they did not know God? To this he answers: They could indeed have known, but they themselves are unwilling, preferring to dwell unjustly in their own pleasure. They detain the truth of God. Because, as is said, that which is known of God is manifest in them; as if to say: they have in themselves whence they may know, namely natural reason. They detain in injustice. What they hold is good, but where they hold it is evil; for they hold the truth, but in iniquity. Have you found God? You have found the truth, and are holding it in injustice; even what you learned through the works of God you have lost through the works of man.
1.19: 1.19 That which is known of God. GREG., book 10 Moral., ch. 4. What is known is what we can attain from the disposition of this world and the natural order. But the unknown of God is what lies hidden from every creature: such as the reason of his substance or nature, and the mystery of human liberation. Is manifest in them. AUG. Because not only natural reason helped to this, but God also assisted daily, lest nature alone should seem sufficient.
1.20: 1.20 From the creature. GREG., book 29 Moral., ch. 8. From man by excellence, because he excels among other creatures, or on account of the agreement he has with all creatures: for he is locally in a place with bodies, he senses with animals, he understands with angels; whence: Preach the Gospel to every creature (Mark 16). When they had known, etc. AUG., Serm. 55 on the Words of the Lord. They saw where they should come, etc., up to for what God had given freely, he took away from the ungrateful.
1.21: 1.21 Was darkened. AMBROSE. For a cloud of error covered their heart, because, though they ought to have honored the Creator the more from the beautiful things which he made, they were dulled, having left him.
1.22: 1.22 They became fools. See how the heart was darkened, which is the vengeance: wise in the natures of things, fools in God.
1.23: 1.23 And they changed. AUG., epist. 119, ch. 6, to Januarius. Here he condemns the images of the ungodly. Some venerated the earth, others the sun and the like. Into the likeness of the image. He heaps up the folly to show the extent of their dullness. Of man and of birds, etc. It was from of old the custom of the Romans to adore images of men, such as Romulus, Jove, and others, especially since the arrival of Aeneas in Italy. Of birds, however, and four-footed beasts and serpents, from the time when Alexandria was conquered by Augustus and subjected to Rome. AMBROSE. For the first Babylonians called the figment of Bel God, etc., up to and birds, because the pagans hold ravens sacred. AUG., book 7 On the City of God, ch. 33. Through this one and true religion (of Christ) it could be disclosed that the gods of the nations are most unclean demons, under the occasion of departed souls or the appearance of worldly creatures, desiring to be thought gods.
1.24: 1.24 He gave them up, etc. AUG., book On Grace and Free Will, ch. 21. It is manifest that God works in the hearts of men to incline their wills, either to good things, according to his mercy, or to evil, according to their deserts, by his judgment, sometimes hidden, sometimes open, but always just. Let them affect. GREG., Homily 11 on Ezekiel. A sin which is not washed away by the lament of penance, etc., up to God permits the blinded mind to slip even into other sins.
1.25: 1.25 Because they changed. He pursues more fully, part by part, the fault and the punishment, that it may appear. Because they changed. He shows that they changed the glory of God part by part, namely that they thought him God who was not, and worshipped and served the creature rather than the Creator. And he pursues the parts of uncleanness: women with women, males with males; in which he matches the punishment to the fault, that as they sinned against the nature of the Creator, so they should be punished in their own nature; whence he concludes: And the reward. They changed the truth. AMBROSE. They gave the name of God, who is true, to those who are not gods. AUG. The truth of the creature is from God, but it is not God, which they turned into a lie, worshipping creatures as the Creator. And they worshipped, etc. But lest they say, I do not worship images, but the things they represent, such as the sun, he adds: And served the creature. Here he condemns what they understood in the images. Amen. As if to say: It is true that to the true God there is blessing for ever; but to the gods of the nations impiety gives honor for a time. Therefore what they say is falsehood.
1.26: 1.26 Passions. That is, pleasures, which, though they delight, are nevertheless passions, not to be called of nature. Natural use. AUG., book 3 Against Julian the Pelagian, ch. 20. Do you think, Julian, that the Apostle praised lust from this, etc., up to is against nature and shameful.
1.27: 1.27 And the reward, etc. AUG. But few see these punishments, etc., up to are sins and punishments. It was fitting. Here the cause for which they were given up is shown without any ambiguity.
1.28: 1.28 And as, etc. Likewise, because they do not yet come to their senses, they fall into others for the same fault. By as, he likens the punishment to the sin, that as they sinned in the sense of God, so they were punished in their own sense. They did not approve. Because they did not know to hold God in knowledge what reason approved; or because they thought God ignorant of and careless about evils. He gave up, etc.
1.29: 1.29 With all iniquity. He enumerates the parts, so as to accuse malice more plainly, when someone contrives harm to another. Wickedness is rashness when one dares what one cannot, or lack of self-control. Contention is the assault on truth through confidence of clamor. Malignity is evil will, when one cannot go further, or does not return thanks for benefits. Detractors: those who deny or pervert the good deeds of others. Hateful to God. Lest whispering or detraction be thought slight because they are in words, he adds of them: Hateful to God, that they may understand that by whispering and detraction alone they can incur eternal damnation. Proud. The proud are those who will not suffer a superior, or an equal.
1.31: 1.31 Disorderly. Disorder of the body indicates the quality of the mind.
1.32: 1.32 Are worthy of death. Lest they be thought to be afflicted only with those punishments in which they delight, he adds the last, eternal death. Who consent to them that do them, etc. To consent is to keep silent when you could reprove; or to foster the error.
2.1: 2.1 Wherefore, etc. This is said commonly of Gentiles and Jews. The Jew judged the Gentile on account of his former state; the Gentile the Jew: each a man, not a spirit. If the Jew judges the Gentile for idolatry, they too are idolaters. If the Gentile judges the Jew for transgression of the law, he too is a transgressor of the natural law. Inexcusable. Because you yourself are a witness of your own condemnation, while you judge another: why? because you do the same things. You who judge. In which he shows himself to be what he is not, that is, just. For you do the same things. The Apostle destroys by his authority the empty excuse of the Gentiles and Jews: for the Jew could offer an excuse for his sin: Even if I do the same things, yet my race and the law defend me as a Jew, ignorance defends me as a Gentile. Against this the Apostle: You who judge, etc. THEOD. It is evident to those who are wise that those who conduct themselves unjustly are punished by the divine sentence.
2.3: 2.3 And do you think. This chapter is commonly read against the Jews and Gentiles; yet it can also be read specially against any haughty prelate of the Church. That you shall escape. You sin when you promise yourself impunity, and more gravely: for you despise the goodness of God, and do not know that you despise it, and do this? A rebuke, as if he said: It is a wonder.
2.4: 2.4 Or do you despise the riches of his goodness. AMBROSE. Copious is the goodness which gives many things and to many, etc., up to but turns it to impunity.
2.5: 2.5 But according to. For there are some to whom the evils they do are displeasing, and, moved by repentance of heart, so far as it is given them to depart from them, they labor: of these he does not speak here. There are others to whom evils are pleasing, and, presuming too much on the mercy of God, they persist obstinately in them, in which they show his patience, and heap up their own burden by sinning worse. There are also others to whom evils are indeed displeasing, but because they understand them to be grave, they think they can no longer be forgiven, like him who said: My iniquity is greater (Gen. 4), etc. The former by excessive hope think God not just; the latter by despair judge God not good. From both, therefore, they will be in danger, by hoping and by despairing, laboring with contrary things and contrary affections, they will perish. Of the just judgment. CYPRIAN. He said that God's judgment is just, etc., up to repentance cannot profit the sinner.
2.6: 2.6 Who will render to every man. Who now does not render to those whom he frees, since toward the wicked his goodness is now generous. But in the future he will render evil for evil, because he is just; good for evil, because he is good and just. He will only not render evil for good, because he is not unjust. GREG. It belongs to justice that they never lack punishment whose mind, etc., up to that man be punished eternally.
2.8: 2.8 Indignation. Lest he seem to be angry and not to avenge: hence tribulation and anguish.
2.9: 2.9 Tribulation and anguish. Meanwhile in the soul alone before the judgment, but after the judgment wrath and indignation. Upon every. What above was indefinite, there: But to them that, here universally, so as to include Jew and Gentile. He says soul, because he is treating of the unbeliever, whose soul will be straitened for its perfidy by spiritual punishment. Of the Jew first. AMBROSE. He always puts the Jew first: because as the believer is more honorable on account of Abraham, so the distrustful is to be treated worse, because he refused the promises made to the fathers.
2.11: 2.11 For there is no, etc. He makes Jew and Gentile equal in punishment and glory: because God judges not according to persons, but according to merits: because he condemns both according to the measure of sin. AMBROSE. God does not follow the prerogative of race so as to receive the distrustful for the fathers' sake, or cast out the believer for the unworthiness of his parents, but rewards or condemns each according to his own merit.
2.12: 2.12 Without the law. AUG. Therefore the Apostle called the Gentiles without the law, because they had not received the written law of Moses, which the Jews boasted of having received. In the law. THE SAME. Those who knew the divine commandments have their excuse taken away, etc., up to or the addition of their own will. Shall be judged. Not that they may be saved as if through fire, as some say, but they will utterly perish. For Christ says that it will be more tolerable for Sodom in the judgment than for the Jews who did not believe in Christ. And again he says that they will have no excuse for the sin of unbelief, because he came and spoke to them: in which they have an excuse, to whom he spoke neither himself nor through his own, who nevertheless will not escape damnation: because he who without the law, etc. They will suffer lighter things, however, because to whom more is committed, from him more is required.
2.13: 2.13 For not the hearers. Does the law alone not save? No, because it does not make men just, and this is: For not for hearing, but whoever are doers, which indeed is by grace. But doers, that is, those who believe in Christ, whom the law promised, whoever they are, which is only by grace. AUG., book On the Spirit and the Letter, ch. 26. The doers of the law shall be justified, that is, shall be reckoned just, or shall be made just; not that those who before were doers shall be justified, because the Gentiles also.
2.14: 2.14 For when, etc. Above he had said that the Gentile is condemned if he does evil, saved if he does good; but since he has not the law, as if he did not know what is good or what is evil, he seems to himself to have to be charged with neither. Against this the Apostle: Though he has not the written law, he has the natural law, by which he understands and is conscious to himself what is good and what is evil; vice indeed is against nature, which grace certainly heals. For the image of earthly affections has not so far worn away in the human soul that no lineaments remain in it. What was impressed there by the image of God when man was created is not wholly destroyed. Hence, the vice being healed by grace, the things of the law are done naturally. Not that grace is denied through nature, but rather that nature is repaired through grace: by which grace, in the inner man renewed, the law of justice is rewritten, which guilt had blotted out.
2.15: 2.15 The work of the law. It is faith, which they have of their own accord in their hearts, that is, in the inmost affection, where faith works by love.
2.17: 2.17 But if you, etc. Here he assails the Jews, accusing them more gravely of sins, because they had more helps.
2.19: 2.19 You are confident. He calls the Gentiles blind and existing in darkness, who, deprived also of reason, are blind; and if they know anything, yet they are in darkness.
2.20: 2.20 Having the form. That you may be to others an example of the knowledge of the law and of the truth. For some have the knowledge and understanding of a certain book and think as the author himself thought, yet they do not have the truth from it: because they do not know how it is true, nor even that it is true; but the Jew boasts that he has the sense of the law, and knows that this sense of the law is true, so that he is a model for others who wish to know.
2.24: 2.24 For the name of God. Among the Gentiles the name of God is blasphemed through the Jews: because the Jews strove to persuade believers that Christ ought not to be called God. Or because formerly the Gentiles did not observe that the Jews had been handed over to them for their own offences, but gave glory to their idols for their victory, as if they had conquered the God of the Jews in the Jews.
2.25: 2.25 Circumcision indeed. He shows above that the law does not help them, now that circumcision does not help to obtain justice. It profits, if the law, etc. Because by obeying God, it makes a sign of truth, while a rude people is kept in the fear of God. It profits. It is asked how he here says circumcision profits, when in what follows he says: If you be circumcised, Christ shall profit you nothing? The answer: This is to be understood according to the state of different times. For according to the state of the old law circumcision once profited, but it did not profit for salvation without the spiritual observance of the law, of which he speaks here. But now, that is, in the time of grace, after the truth has been shown, it not only does not profit but even harms, of which in what follows.
2.26: 2.26 Shall not. The Gentile, by comparison with himself, shows you, O Jew, to be damnable, who know through the law, not through nature nor through circumcision, what he knows through nature, that is, Christ?
2.27: 2.27 Shall judge, etc. ORIG. Circumcision is in the flesh. To circumcise is from the genital member, etc., up to in whom there is not the circumcision of the flesh, but the observance of the law.
2.28: 2.28 For not. As if: A Gentile can well become a Jew, and a Jew a Gentile, as has been said. A Jew. Is interpreted confessing: for he who truly believes and rightly confesses is truly a Jew.
2.29: 2.29 Circumcision of the heart. ORIG. It is that which purifies the soul and cuts away the stains of vices. Whose praise. AMBROSE. God praises the believer, etc., up to which appeared before men in the work. Not of men. AUG. He calls it circumcision of the heart, namely a will pure from all unlawful concupiscence: which is done not by the letter teaching and threatening, but by the Spirit helping and healing.
3.1: 3.1 What advantage then. He raises against himself what he sees can be raised, in order to resolve it. Since the Jew becomes a Gentile and the reverse. Then what is more to the Jew, who is called the peculiar people of God, than to the Gentile, who is called an unclean dog? or what has he gained from circumcision? To this he answers: It did avail once, but they are not therefore more worthy in the faith, and this is: Much more is there to the Jew according to the former state than to the Gentile, and this in every way. Every way is either in the administration of temporal things or in the unlocking of spiritual things, in both of which God did many things for the Jews which he did not for the Gentiles; and so according to the former state they were more worthy.
3.2: 3.2 First indeed, etc. As if: To pass over other lesser matters of temporal things, I put this first and chief, that the oracles of God, that is, the law and the prophets, were entrusted to them as friends, through which they might understand the redemption to come. But you will say: More was not therefore done for them, because they did not believe the oracles, so that some of them might receive the promised Christ. To this it is answered: It did not therefore profit the believers less, and this is: For if some of them have not believed, shall their unbelief make the faith of God without effect?
3.3: 3.3 Shall their unbelief. AMBROSE. No, he says, because some were unwilling to believe, prejudice will not be done to the rest of the Jews, that they should not be called worthy to receive what God promised to the faithful, since the promise was so made that it should profit those who believe. Faith. ORIG. We understand that which God has with those to whom he entrusts his oracles, or that by which some believe God.
3.4: 3.4 But every. He adds this to make it appear that the promise of God was made and fulfilled, not on account of any dignity of man, but on account of mercy: so that grace is given to the unworthy, and grace is more commendable. But God is called true, that is, unchangeable, as much in essence as in promise. Man a liar, that is, not having true being of nature, and falling away through sins. Every man a liar. He who denies that God has fulfilled the promises: this especially the Jew, whom God overcomes when he gives the promises. Every man. Even the Jew, lest he seem more worthy in the new state than the Gentile.
3.5: 3.5 But if our injustice. He said that God is true and every man a liar, and that he gives good things to the unworthy, in which his justice and grace appear more commendable: hence the carnal man, saying that God uses evil as an instrument for his glory, brings the matter to this, that he calls God unjust who punishes sins which serve him. This he removes, saying: Is God unjust. God true and man a liar. But if this is so, and thus our injustice commends the justice of God, what seems to follow? That God is unjust. But is God unjust who inflicts evils?
3.7: 3.7 For if the truth. The removal of the injustice of God having been interposed, the Apostle returns to the refutation of the carnal man who strives to prove that God is unjust if he punishes the wicked, because if he is the more glorious for it: why am I also still, and not only in the future, judged as a sinner, which I am not? Or: Yet, that is, after conversion, after he gave gifts to the unworthy. For when before I deserved badly from my own deeds, he was not more glorious: as if he said: What could seem so before forgiveness ought not to seem so after, namely that I should be judged a sinner, as if to say: It is certain that the truth of forgiving would not have abounded to glory unless I had sinned.
3.8: 3.8 And not as. As if: And if it is this, that the truth of God abounds in sin, why do we not do evil that good may come, as it is imputed to us to think this (which is blasphemy) and even to preach on the occasion of such words: Where sin abounded, grace did more abound? Or: Let it be joined more closely to the preceding text than before. As if: How will God judge? As if: Not rightly, for neither would he now justly judge me as a sinner, which I am not, and truly not.
3.9: 3.9 What then. As if: He did more for the Jew in the former state; and, because he fulfilled good things for them not from any merit of theirs. What then? do we excel them? Truly, since every man is a liar; therefore we Jews do not excel the Gentiles in this state of grace, although we were more excellent in the former state in every way. No means. Because there is no respect of persons with God, but in every nation he that fears God is acceptable to him (Acts 10).
3.11: 3.11 There is none that seeks. From the works they could have sought and found that Christ was God.
3.12: 3.12 They are all gone aside, etc. It does not signify the whole people altogether, but the other part of the people. For there are always two peoples in one people: whence Jeremias: Then all rose up against the prophet of the Lord, wishing to kill him. And he added: But all the people did not suffer them (Jer. 38). He said all rose up, that is, the wicked; that all the people did not suffer them, namely the good. There is not so much as one. For Christ alone does good in himself and in his own.
3.15: 3.15 Their feet are swift. Of whom the Lord: Jerusalem, Jerusalem, that kill the prophets (Matt. 23). And again: A wicked and adulterous generation (ibid. 16). And of whom Isaias: Woe to the sinful nation, a wicked seed (Isa. 1), etc.
3.16: 3.16 Destruction. They do such things whereby they are crushed in this world, through Titus and Vespasian, and in the future they will be unhappy, punished in soul and body.
3.19: 3.19 In the law. The law is sometimes called generally the Old Testament, as there: The Lord opened to the disciples the sense, that they might understand the things concerning him which were written in the law and the prophets and the psalms (Luke 24; John 10; Ps. 81). Sometimes the psalms are called law. As the Lord says: It is written in your law: I said you are gods and all of you sons of the Most High. And elsewhere: That the word may be fulfilled which is written in their law: They hated me without cause (John 15; Ps. 34). That every mouth may be stopped, even of the Jews boasting of their glory, that they came to the faith by their merits; or let the mouth of the Jews be so stopped, as above that of the Gentiles who boasted of their good nature.
3.20: 3.20 Because by the works. As he took away glory from circumcision, so he wishes to do with the other works of the law. And it is a new sentence, though joined to the preceding by: Because by the works of the law, etc. Works of the law are called those which were instituted and limited in the law, such as were the ceremonial and figurative ones, which never availed to cleanse the conscience, even if done with charity and devotion, because they were not instituted for justification, but for the signifying of things to come and for showing the weakness of sin, because the law did not come to take away sins, but to show and punish them. No flesh shall be justified, etc. Understand this of the ceremonial works, not the moral, which certainly justify and are consummated in the Gospel. In his sight. Who sees the inmost things, namely whether something is done from love of justice or from fear of punishment, which men do not see. For by the law. Here he begins about the law, to show that justice is not from it. For by the law is the knowledge of sin. He says this, not that sins were not known before, but that all things were known by the law not to be going to go unpunished before God. Some sins were known before the law, as when Joseph, accused before Pharao of the crime of adultery, was sent to prison. And his brothers said: We deservedly suffer these things, because we have sinned against our brother (Gen. 39). But some were known through the law that were unknown before, such as concupiscence and original sin. Some also graver were known through the law than they had been thought before.
3.21: 3.21 Being witnessed, etc. Because the law figured it by many sacraments, by that very fact it bears witness to the justice of God, because in it no one is justified. The prophets bear witness, by foretelling that which the coming of Christ fulfilled.
3.22: 3.22 Even the justice, etc. Not that by which he himself is just essentially, but that with which he clothes the ungodly: when he mercifully makes a believer of an unbeliever. It is called the justice of God, which more properly seems to be called mercy, because it has its origin in promise: and when the promise of God is paid, it is called the justice of God. For it is justice because what was promised has been paid; and when he receives those who flee to him it is called the justice of God, because not to receive them would be iniquity.
3.23: 3.23 Need the glory, that is, the indulgence and pardon of sins.
3.24: 3.24 Justified freely. Not by the law, not by one's own will, but by the grace of Christ, yet not so that it is done without our will. But our will is shown to be weak through the law: so that grace may heal the will, and the healed will fulfill the law, not set under the law nor needing the law. Freely, that is, with no merits of works preceding, otherwise grace is no more grace, since it is given not because we have done good works, but that we may be able to do them.
3.25: 3.25 Whom God has proposed, etc. To the end that he might show himself truthful in his promises, which showing was necessary not only for the remission of present sins but also of those that went before in the forbearance of God, God namely bearing and not punishing, and also to show in this time of Christ what could not be done at any other time, that he himself may be just and the justifier of him who is of the faith of Jesus. Faith in his blood, that is, faith of the passion, or through faith and through the passion: for neither avails without the other. For the remission. The effect of remission is twofold, namely to be free from punishment and to enjoy glory. The first the just had before the death of Christ, because they did not feel actual punishment. But after the death of Christ the glory of the divine vision was given them, from which they were put off while God bore their offences.
3.26: 3.26 In the forbearance. God patiently bore the sins of those who were before the law and under the law: he neither punished nor remitted them so that they should have glory, until he came who would absolve the offences, both of those who went before and of those who followed, at the price of his blood.
3.27: 3.27 Is excluded. Whether he meant the praiseworthy glorying which is in the Lord, and that it is excluded, not that it should depart, being driven out, but that it should stand out, being expressed. Hence also silversmiths are called excluders; whence the Psalmist: That they may be excluded who are proved with silver (Ps. 67), etc. Or if he wished to recall faulty glorying, he says it is excluded by the law of faith, that is, cast out and thrown away, because by the law of faith each one knows that if he lives well in any way, he has it by the grace of God.
3.28: 3.28 That a man is justified. Not that the believer afterwards ought not to work by love, as Abraham also was willing to sacrifice his son. For works follow the justified, they do not precede the one to be justified, but by faith alone, without preceding works, a man is made just, so that those who had done the works of the law out of fear are no more just, since faith works by love in the heart, even if it does not go out in work outwardly. Hence it is not by the merits of previous works that one comes to the justice of faith, in which the Jews preferred themselves. For the good works that are called such before faith are empty, so that they seem to be great strength and a swift course off the road. Where faith was not, there was no good work. For intention makes the work good, faith directs the intention. Without works. Preceding, not following, without which faith is empty, as James says: Faith without works is dead (James 2); and Paul himself: If I should have all faith (1 Cor. 13), etc. Through faith. AUG., Enchir., ch. 107. This is the faith of Christ which the Apostle commends, which works by love.
3.31: 3.31 God forbid. For the law is not destroyed, when, fulfilled according to the spirit, it ceases according to the letter. We establish. Because we have shown fulfilled what the law says; or we establish, that is, we make firm, because this is the grace of faith, by which the law is fulfilled, the law which without faith would be weak. For the status of the law is made firm, because the mystical and ceremonial things are spiritually fulfilled, and what was lacking in the moral things is added in the Gospel; and what the law promised would come, the faith of the Gospel testifies has come. The mystical and promising things, then, are fulfilled in the Gospel according to spiritual understanding, but the killing letter is taken away.
4.1: 4.1 According to the flesh. That is, from the works of the law. As if to say: Shall we say that he was just from them? No, because if he is just from carnal observance, he has the eternal glory that follows from justice: but he has it from himself, not from God. Or, this justification is in the opinion of men, and not before God. But toward God he has glory: therefore he was not justified from works. If, then, he was not justified from works, whence was he justified? It follows and says whence, etc.
4.3: 4.3 Believed. To believe was a sufficient cause of justice for him, and is for others; but nevertheless to him who has time for working, the reward will not be given according to grace only, but according to the debt of his work; but to him who has not time for working, if he believes, faith alone suffices for justice, and so for salvation, according to the grace proposed to all, or according to what God laid down before in the law.
4.4: 4.4 Now to him, etc. As if to say: Abraham is just from faith: but to him who does those carnal works, or some good works to merit grace, if the reward is for him, it is not of grace, but of the debt of his merit. But to him who does not do these carnal works or any good works, but only believes, faith suffices for justice, and so he attributes to others what he said of Abraham, namely that if he is just from works, he has glory, but not before God, and therefore from faith. According to grace. If it is grace, it is given freely or stands freely. You have done no good, and forgiveness of sins is given to you. Your works are attended to and are all found evil. But according to debt. AUG. Do not flatter yourself about merits, etc., up to let us do by his gift and bounty.
4.5: 4.5 But to him that believes, etc. He does not say, him. For he believes him who believes that the things he speaks are true, which the wicked also do. To believe him is to believe that he is God, which the devils also do. But to believe in him is by believing to love him, by believing to esteem him, by believing to go into him, and to be incorporated into his members. According to the purpose. As if to say: Without preceding works the ungodly is justified, and this according to the purpose of the grace of God, that is, according to the grace of God proposed to all believers, or according to what God laid down long before.
4.7: 4.7 Forgiven. To forgive, to cover, not to impute are words of the same reason and sense. Iniquities. By iniquities is understood original sin, namely the fomes of sin, which is called concupiscence or concupiscibility, or the law of the members, or the languor of nature, and by other names. And before baptism it is guilt and punishment, but after baptism punishment and not guilt, which makes a little child capable of concupiscing, but not concupiscing; an adult, however, even concupiscing, which indeed is forgiven in baptism and passes away as to liability, but remains as to act. It is called original, however, because it is drawn from the vicious condition of our origin, and because we are conceived by the vicious law of conceiving, arising from the sin of the first man, that is, the concupiscence of the flesh, therefore we are guilty of sin, which is called original. Sins are covered. AUG. Do not understand what he said: sins are covered, as if they were there and lived. He said covered, then, so that they might not be seen, but for God to see sin is to punish it.
4.9: 4.9 In circumcision, that is, at the time of circumcision, faith was reckoned to Abraham unto justice.
4.10: 4.10 But in uncircumcision, that is, at the time of uncircumcision.
4.13: 4.13 For not through the law the promise. Other promises were made to Christ than to Abraham. For those made to Abraham were such that those who imitated him in this way would be blessed by Christ; but to Christ not so, but in such a way that he should be not only the exemplar and form of the instruction of morals and works, but should bless with eternal blessing those who imitate him. To his seed. That is, to all believers, who are the seed of Abraham, not by flesh but by imitation. Or to Christ, to whom the promise is said to have been made, because it was to be fulfilled in him.
4.14: 4.14 For if, etc. As if to say: Truly Abraham is not heir of the world through the law: because his sons through the law are not those who, called sons, are heirs, namely who possess what he has. For if this were so, these inconveniences would follow from it: that faith would be made void, by which it is established that Abraham was just; that the promise would be abolished, that is, unfulfilled, so that there would be no heirs: for the law makes no heirs, for it rather works wrath, and so transgression; for from it is transgression, because without it there is none. Therefore because if these things followed from the law: then they are heirs from faith, and so the promise is firm.
4.15: 4.15 The law works wrath. That it might make offenders guilty, not as efficient cause, but because grace did not help; or it would make them guilty of temporal punishments, it would work wrath, because transgression, how this is, he opens, saying: For where, etc. ORIG. He shows that there cannot be transgression unless there was a law; yet if there is a law, there will not be transgression in every kind: for it can happen that there is a law and no transgression, but not the converse. Neither transgression. He does not say: There is no iniquity. For everyone who passes over the law is unjust, but not the converse. For those who have not received the law can be called unjust, but cannot be called transgressors.
4.16: 4.16 Not to him who is of the law. Because such a one falls from grace, and therefore for the sake of faith one must withdraw from the law, that the promise may be firm: for the law without the grace of promise not only does not take away sin, but even increases it.
4.18: 4.18 Who against hope. He begins to commend the faith of Abraham, that we may imitate him who through faith received justice and such a promise. So shall your seed be, etc. It is to be known that Abraham first knew God as three and one, and by this merit of faith obtained the remission of all sins. After justice, however, he received from God the promise that he would become the father of many nations. Then a promise was made to him again that his seed would be as the stars, etc.
4.19: 4.19 He was not weakened. Some, puffed up by worldly reason, neglected God: therefore what is impossible to the world, God did, that through these things believers might be saved.
4.20: 4.20 In the promise. Isaac, promised contrary to the nature of human generation, was a sign that the Son of God would be born of man contrary to human nature; and that the sons of men, through the spirit of regeneration, would be begotten from sinners as sons of God, from mortals as immortals.
4.24: 4.24 In him that raised up Jesus, etc. He has fittingly begun the discourse about the Lord, and says: He did not die for his own sins, for in this way he ought not to have risen, as neither did anyone before him, but for our sins, that he might free us from them. As also he restored to life, and to the procreation of children, the womb of Abraham and Sara, already dead through old age and barrenness.
4.25: 4.25 Who was delivered. The death of Christ alone signifies the destruction of the old life, and in the resurrection alone is signified the new life, which begins from justification and will be perfected in immortality.
5.1: 5.1 From faith. Above he said, justified freely by grace, lest faith itself be proud. Let not the faithful man say: I have faith that I may deserve justification; for it is answered him: What have you that you have not received? Let us have peace, we who are reconciled to him through the minister of grace, Christ.
5.2: 5.2 By whom. He enumerates the benefits which are had from Christ.
5.3: 5.3 Tribulation. That tribulation does not take away patience, charity does, which is the proper gift of the Holy Spirit. Hope. That is, the certainty of future glory, which seems vain to human reason: but is made firm by the testimony of virtue, that is, of patience or of miracles.
5.5: 5.5 And hope. Because it is in God who does not deceive, not in man the liar, of whose hope the pledge is the Spirit: for it is read: Let your fountain of water be your own, and let no stranger communicate with you (Ecclus. 5); this is the Spirit, whom the wicked cannot receive, and it is charity, which a wicked man cannot have. But to have the name of Christ and baptism, to receive the body of the Lord, and to have the other sacraments, one can be wicked. Charity, therefore, is the proper gift of the Spirit, and a singular fountain. The charity of God. Or God loves us widely: and this we have in our hearts through the Spirit who makes us understand the charity of God toward us.
5.6: 5.6 For why. Since God loves us, or we him through the Spirit, hope will be fulfilled: because unless it were so, Christ suffered in vain. And this is why Christ died for the ungodly, that is, out of love for the ungodly or in their stead, for the ungodly, not those who had been so long ago and were not then, but when we were weak in sins. According to the time, that is, for three days only, lest you despair of the power of him whose goodwill appears in death: from whom we receive such pledges, that he gave his death to the ungodly, who keeps his life for the just. He died for you, O mortal man, that you may live with him. He took on our death, that he might give us his life: he took from you that from which he might die for you. He put himself on, wherein he might die for you: he will put you on, wherein you may live with him. He put himself on mortal flesh in the virginity of his mother: he will put you on in eternal life in the equality of the Father.
5.7: 5.7 Scarcely. He says, for a just man. Perhaps for a good man: he shows both to be difficult and rare, but one more difficult and rarer. For a just man, etc. A just man by exercise, who is also good; but there is also a good man who is not just, that is, who was born in simplicity: the innocent who has not yet labored to enlarge himself in good things, as are little children cleansed in baptism; and though the just is better, yet on account of innocence he is more pitiable than on account of justice, because justice of this kind is not without severity.
5.8: 5.8 While as yet. Behold, while he hated according to sins, he loved according to his own work: which he also did before the foundation of the world. It had to be told how much he loved us, lest we despair; and what sort we were, lest we be proud. There was also another way possible to God, who can do all things, but none more suitable for healing our misery. For what so lifts us up, and frees us from despair of immortality, as that he made so much of us that a man died for us?
5.9: 5.9 Much more therefore. It is harder to die for sin and take away sin than to save the already just who also cooperate. In his blood. Because thus the devil is overcome by justice, not by power. By justice, because the devil killed one undeserving, namely Christ: whence he justly loses others also. Not by power, because the devil is a lover of power and a deserter of justice, in which men more imitate him. It pleased God, therefore, that not by power but by justice, conquering, he should rescue man, in which man might imitate him: but afterwards, in the resurrection, power followed, because the dead one lived again, never to die afterwards.
5.10: 5.10 We were enemies. Not sinners in just any way. We are reconciled. Because before we were justly under the power of the devil, our nature depraved by sin.
5.12: 5.12 Wherefore. He said that through Christ there is justice and life. And that it can be through him, he intends to prove by likeness in the lesser. By one. Adam, namely; the Apostle did not say one Eve: keeping the custom, since he attributes the succession of human posterity (which succumbs to sin and death coming from him) not to the woman but to the man. For posterity is wont to be named not from the woman but from the man. Or because the woman is from the man, and of both one flesh. Whether, then, it be said from Eve or from Adam, both pertain to the first man: and by this the Apostle wished original sin to be understood as of propagation, whose prince is Adam, not of imitation, whose prince is the devil; whence: By the envy of the devil, death entered into this world. Upon all men. Because even before the law, when it did not so appear, the law not teaching, sin was indeed imputed among men, but not before God, as the sinners thought, with whom it was thought it would be unpunished, since it was not known that he would judge: but when the law was given, they knew that God cares for human things and judges. Before, it was not imputed, but death reigned securely, the devil possessing men, with impunity believed, until Moses, through whom the knowledge of the one God returned. Death therefore reigned (as another reading has), not however over all, but over those like the transgressor Adam, who, neglecting God, served the creature, as he in the place of God consented to the devil. Such were almost all until the law. Very few, like Abraham, served the one God, and over them death did not reign, but rather under hope they were kept to be freed at the coming of Christ.
5.13: 5.13 Until the law, etc. That is, because neither could the law take away sin, but it increased it, whether natural or written: but it was not imputed, that is, it was unknown: yet it reigned until Moses, that is, the law: because not even the law itself could take away the reign of death, which reigns while it does not allow the guilt of sin to come to eternal life, but drags to Gehenna. This reign the grace of Christ alone destroyed, even in the ancients: apart from whom it reigned over all: even over those who did not sin by their own will, like Adam, but were held by original vice, like children.
5.14: 5.14 But death reigned. It was not imputed, but the effect showed it, because bodily death reigned daily through some sufferings, at length dissolving, until Moses, when it seemed less. Who is the figure. Adam is the figure of Christ: because as he is the father of all according to the flesh, so Christ according to faith; and as from his side Eve was formed, so from this one's side flowed the sacraments, by which the Church is saved. And therefore as he could communicate to his sons sin and death, so this one to his own his justice and life, and also this one confers more good on his own than that one evil: and therefore he can save more than that one destroy.
5.15: 5.15 But not as, etc. The figure is in this, that one amends, one sinned, but the case of Adam is not such as that of Christ: because the offence of Adam is one, by which many, that is, those similarly transgressing, are dead, but the grace of Christ is to more: because to these and to those not similarly transgressing.
5.17: 5.17 For if. AMBROSE. Death reigned, it does not reign, because he who through the law, etc., up to for there is not a general condemnation or justification in all. By one reigned, etc. Because the powers which he had in him, he exercised on all posterity, of whom he was the matter: as also the fault, which was his alone, was transfused into all. Much more, etc. Because eternally, whereas death reigned in them temporally and with an end.
5.18: 5.18 By the justice of one, etc. Not that all begotten from Adam are regenerated through Christ, but as no one's carnal generation is except through Adam, so no one's spiritual except through Christ. If there were any begotten apart from Adam, and any regenerated apart from Christ, he would not say all and all. But as no man is apart from that generation, so no one is just apart from this. The same he afterwards calls many.
5.19: 5.19 For as, etc. He determines the offence of one and the justice of one, that as the former lost by the merit of sin, so this one seems to have freed us by the merit of justice. So also by the obedience of one, etc. He says of a man, not of God or of the Word, lest you think that the ancient just were freed by the Word of God alone, that is, by faith in the Word alone without faith in the incarnation.
5.20: 5.20 Now the law, etc. He had shown that Christ forgives all sins, both original and actual: here he adds that he also frees from the sin of the law, that is, transgression, so that the Jews may be more obliged to Christ; as if to say: The first is justification, but the law entered in secretly. AMBROSE. The Apostle says here what came about when the law was given, etc., up to God forgave all. The law entered in. To those born in sins the law is given to tame pride, as if: There is no lack of one to command, but of one to fulfill, because one born in sin cannot fulfill: therefore Christ was born, that is, the grace that would heal. That sin might abound. That is, that he who was in filth might by transgressing become filthier, that the middling might have a pedagogue, the perfect a sign, and the hard feel the scourge. Did more abound. Because the grace of Christ also profits those whom the devil could not conquer: and because sin reigned for a time, grace for ever.
5.21: 5.21 As sin has reigned unto death. He does not add, through one or through Adam: because he is not treating only of what men drew from Adam, but also of what they added by their own will. But when he says: Grace may reign, he adds, through Jesus Christ, etc., because through him there is remission of sins, not only original but also voluntary.
6.1: 6.1 Shall we abide. The perverse take this from that: Where sin abounded, grace did more abound. To say this is to be ungrateful to grace. And because grace flourishes where sin abounded, one must not remain in sin, as some think for the sake of greater grace. For grace did more abound where sin abounded not by the merit of the sinner, but by the help of the one who came to his aid. We must not, then, remain in sin, but rather we ought and can be, to sin, as it were dead and buried through grace itself, and rise again unto justice, and afterwards to eternal life.
6.2: 6.2 We are dead. That is, freed from sin through baptism, so that it no longer rules in us through grace. For to die to sin is to be freed from sin. How shall we, etc. For when grace has provided this, that we should die to sin, what else do we do if we live in it, but that we are ungrateful to grace?
6.3: 6.3 Know you not. Having died to sin, which is done in baptism, we ought not to live to it again, so that it would again be necessary to die to it: because in the death of Christ, that is, in the likeness of the death of Christ, that as he died once in the flesh and lives always, so we, once dead to evil through baptism, may live always to good. Or he says in death: because death is the cause of this purification.
6.4: 6.4 Buried together. Whatever was done in the cross of Christ, in the burial, in the resurrection, in the ascension, in the sitting at the right hand, was so done that by these things, mystically not only spoken but also done, the Christian life is configured. Consider each of Christ's acts, who had lived as the old man according to punishment, hunger, thirst and the like, not according to guilt: in this way he ended and arranged oldness, so that, enduring the pain of the cross, he thus had his members stretched out and fixed, that they should not move to former acts, from which also, buried, he rested, withdrawn from human sight, demanding of us that we lay aside the oldness of sins with sorrow and groaning of penance: that the members be fixed through continence and justice, that we not return to former evils, from which we may so perfectly rest that neither the sight nor the memory of them be held: and not only does he demand this of us in the sacrament of the passion, but he also effects it, if we wish to imitate him. He rose from the dead. The death and resurrection of Christ are also sacraments.
6.6: 6.6 The old man. That is, the old acts are crucified, that is, dead. Our oldness and curse consists in two things, namely guilt and punishment. Christ, however, with his single oldness consumed our double. For in the sepulchre he rested one day and two nights. By the one day his single oldness is signified, by the two nights our twofold; whence: Christ blotted out our guilt, present, past, and future. The past by forgiving, the present by drawing us back from it, the future by conferring grace that we might avoid it. The punishment also he likewise consumed, utterly deleting the punishment of Gehenna, so that those truly penitent do not feel it. The temporal, however, he did not wholly remove: for hunger, thirst, death and the like remain; but he cast down its kingdom and dominion, and in the last will utterly exterminate it.
6.9: 6.9 Knowing that Christ. AUG. One rose, no more to die. Lazarus rose, but to die; the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue rose, but to die; the widow's son rose, but to die: Christ rose, not to die. Hear the Apostle, Christ rising again, etc. Hope for such a resurrection, and for this be a Christian, not for the happiness of this earth.
6.10: 6.10 For in that he died to sin. AUG. The Apostle commends the sacrament of baptism, that as he by dying once is proclaimed dead in the likeness of sin, so whoever has been baptized in him may die to the same thing of which that was the likeness, that is, to sin; and may live, being born again from the font, as he by rising from the sepulchre.
6.11: 6.11 So do you also. Whatever he said above belongs to men through the grace of Christ, here he attributes to the Romans.
6.12: 6.12 Let not sin therefore. Because he said above that we are dead to sins and ought not to live in it, since no one is without sin: he determines what is chiefly to be guarded against, as if concluding what was asked above: Shall we abide in sin. That you obey the lusts. Concupiscence is sometimes the name of the fomes, namely of an inborn vice; sometimes of an interior act, which is also in the first motion, which is called propassion, and in the second which is called delectation, and in the third which is called consent. Here he does not forbid concupiscence which is in the first motion, because it is not in our power when it arises: but by the grace of God we can restrain it, that it not come to delectation and consent, which he forbids.
6.15: 6.15 What then? Because the law is from God, he sins who abandons it for grace. What then? Shall we sin. Because we are not under the law, which terrifies, but under grace, which promises well? What then? shall we sin? This some say, who preach the law as binding or constraining, and to be held.
6.16: 6.16 Know you not that, etc. Lest, professing God in words, we become the devil's, he warns us that we are servants of him whose will we do.
6.17: 6.17 But thanks be to God, etc. He both shows their change and makes known how pleasing this is to him, offering a hymn to God. For you were, he says, servants of sin: but of your own will and free choice of mind you shook off its dominion, and embraced spiritual doctrine. The form of doctrine. Our doctrine is a form, which restores the deformed image of God.
6.19: 6.19 I speak a human thing, etc. Thus far the Apostle has shown that one must not sin. Here he says what must be done thereafter, namely that justice be served, of which there is no one who can excuse himself, because there is no one who cannot do good, at least in will: which is the same through grace. For as you have yielded, etc. AUG. If not more, or as much as then, lest the faith be shunned as harsh and unbearable. As then no fear compelled, but lust and the pleasure of sin led, so now the delight of justice, grown up, though not yet perfect; whence he said: A human thing. So now. Because justice ought to be loved even more than iniquity was then, so that for justice man would endure sorrows and despise all things, even death.
6.20: 6.20 Free. The freedom of a servant is when sinning delights him, which is from free will. He serves freely who gladly does the will of the Lord; so also he serves justice freely who loves, who rejoices.
6.21: 6.21 What fruit therefore. This remembering makes former things abhorred, and makes men more indebted to grace. You are ashamed. For there is a certain temporal confusion, namely the disturbance of a mind looking back at its sins, and shuddering at the looking back, and blushing at the shuddering, and correcting by blushing. The end of them, etc. Because death is the worthy retribution for sin: but eternal life, which is the end of the just, is given by grace alone through Christ, because merits also are from grace, and grace shall be rendered for grace.
6.22: 6.22 But now being freed. AUG. He said free to justice, not freed: now not free from sin, lest they attribute this to themselves, but he says freed accordingly, according to the saying of the Lord: If the Son shall make you free, you shall be free indeed (John 8). The wages. Rightly wages, because eternal death is rendered to the service of the devil as a debt. To whom would the just Judge render the crown, if the merciful Father had not given grace? how would that debt be paid, unless that grace were first freely given? AUG. Since sins had separated the human race far from God, we needed to be reconciled through a mediator, who alone was born without sin, lived and was slain, so that both human pride might be convicted and healed by the humility of God, and it might be shown to man how far he had departed from God, etc.
7.1: 7.1 Know you not. Thus far of the force of grace: now, that the law is no longer to be held, and he treats of the end of the law, and of its former uselessness: let not the Romans, therefore, wonder that the Apostle says: You are not under the law, but under grace: above it was said that it does not justify, here that it ought to cease; because it was given until Christ. The order: Know you not this, namely: that the natural law has dominion over a man as long as he lives, which you ought not to be ignorant of; for you know the law, and I speak to those who know the law? in which what I say is made manifest, if it be understood spiritually, or the law of Moses has dominion over a man, that he obey it; for you also know the law of Moses, for to those who know, etc. And so the letter can be read in two ways, either of the natural law, or of the Mosaic law. Lives. For the law is said to be dead when its authority ceases.
7.2: 7.2 For the woman that has a husband. To strengthen their minds, he uses the example of human law. The Romans know the law, because they are not barbarians, but have comprehended natural justice, partly from the Greeks, as the Greeks and Hebrews.
7.3: 7.3 Therefore, while her husband lives, etc. If, keeping the dead law, she wishes to belong to faith, she is an adulteress in both, and Christ does not profit her. But if her husband be dead. So the law being finished, he who passes to Christ, the figures being laid aside, does not transgress.
7.4: 7.4 By the body of Christ. Because Christ was the fulfillment and truth: the legal things were the figure and shadow of Christ, and of those things which are fulfilled in Christ.
7.5: 7.5 For when we were. Here he sets down four states of man: before the law, under the law, under grace: then in the other life where there is no war.
7.6: 7.6 But now, etc. AUG. In the preceding likeness there are three: the husband, etc., up to that they may not conquer it. From the law of death. For concupiscence was increased when the law forbade where there was no faith, and to the heap of sins was added the crime of transgression; because where there is no law, neither is there transgression. In newness of spirit. In the works of the new man, which we attain not by our own strength or by the law, but by grace, namely of the spirit, in which we must so abide that nothing be added from the works of the law, which are old.
7.7: 7.7 What shall we say then. Since the law is of death and increased the strength of sin, holding back from good working; the law therefore seems to be sin, that is, teaching to sin, or such that its author sinned in giving it, as of an evil thing. No, but rather it is good: it made sin known, because before it was not known that some things were sins, or so grave, or to be punished. God forbid. But sin. He shows that the law is not sin, but the indicator of sin: so that thus the soul, by anxiety of guilt, might be turned to receive grace. AUG. God forbid. With one word he acquits the law, etc., up to great is the authority of the Apostle defending. THEOD. But that, I knew not, and I was ignorant, do not here signify ignorance altogether, but this he says: I took through the law a more exact knowledge of natural discernment. For concupiscence. The Apostle reads this as general, whence all things. Good is the law, which in forbidding this forbids all. Concupiscence. Some understand it as general. Others that of which in the Decalogue: You shall not covet your neighbor's house or his wife (Exod. 20). General, because from it comes all evil. I knew not. In his own person he pleads the general cause.
7.8: 7.8 But sin taking occasion. Because such is our carnality that it desires the forbidden more ardently: which, if not mentioned, would lie as if asleep. And the devil, seeing the law given as a help to men, burned the more and pressed on the more, to turn it for them into destruction, whereas before, possessing as if securely, he tempted less; or occasion taken in the very things, as when a woman or gold was seen. AUG. Concupiscence was less when before the law you sinned securely, etc., up to is every, when it transgresses the law. AMBROSE. Saying all concupiscence, he signifies all sins. For it was before sin, but not every kind, when the crime of transgression was still lacking. But every sin has now come, because also transgression. AUG. For concupiscence was increased by the prohibition of the law, when grace was still lacking to free.
7.9: 7.9 And I lived. It is plain: because he speaks not from his own person, but of man in general. And I lived. Note two men in the same, the inner and the outer, that is, reason and the fomes, which is in the flesh. The inner he says consents to the law, and by its testimony approves the law as good. The outer, however, fights against the inner and against the law, and takes captive, and through the law has greater power of sinning. But when the commandment came, etc. Here is the second state, under the law. That is: Here the Apostle speaks in the state of man placed under the law. Revived. It began to appear and to rebel. Revived, he says, not lived. For it had lived once in paradise, when it was sufficiently evident that it was committed against the commandment given. But when men born sinners lived without commandment, like something dead it lay hid without knowledge, because without restraint: but the law being given, it revived in man's knowledge, having once lived in the knowledge of the first man.
7.10: 7.10 Found. Before, he was unknown to himself as a sinner, but now he has become manifest to himself as a transgressor. For. As if to say: How was it given to me unto death? Because through it I was seduced by a false sweetness. Taking occasion, etc. What is desired becomes sweeter while it is forbidden, and so sin deceives through the commandment. From the prohibition, for where charity fails the desire of evil grows: and this being done, what is forbidden becomes sweeter, and so it deceives with false sweetness. For deceitful is the sweetness which many and greater bitternesses of punishment follow. Seduced. It drew from good to evil, and through this led to eternal damnation. Killed. AUG. With your sword which you were carrying, etc., up to be therefore humble and you will be able to conquer.
7.12: 7.12 Wherefore the law indeed. It itself is holy, teaching rightly. And the commandment, that is, what is commanded through it. Holy, in itself. And just, that is, justifying the sinner. And good. That is, useful, acquiring life. And since it is clear to me that the law is good, and yet from it death comes to me, as was said above, has therefore that which is good been made death, that is, is it given to me by God so that it is the efficient cause of death? No: but the fomes is the efficient cause, which turns a good thing into evil.
7.13: 7.13 That sin may appear. I do not say, that it may be, because it also was, when it did not appear, as above. I knew not concupiscence. He did not say, I had not. By that which is good. The law. Not certainly causing sin, but rather showing and forbidding it. That it may become exceeding. Because through the law it did not fail, but rather grew beyond accustomed desires.
7.14: 7.14 But I. Thus far he has excused the law, that the fault ought not to be poured back upon it; here he says that neither upon the principal nature, that is reason, according to what it has from God; and so not upon the Creator, but upon men, who are of themselves vitiated, so that they cannot resist perverse motions. I am carnal. Not unbecomingly does the Apostle say this even of himself, according to the flesh as long as he lives here, on account of the motions of the flesh. And every saint says this well. Sold under sin. And this from the fault of the first man, who for the delight of the forbidden food sold himself and all others. Or, under sin, that is, they are servants of sin. Or each one sold himself by the custom of his own will.
7.16: 7.16 For what I work. He proves that he is a servant of sin: because what I work according to the outer man, leaving good undone or doing evil, I understand according to the inner man is not to be worked. Truly I work what I understand not, because I both leave the good which I will and do the evil which I will not. I understand not. Because I see that I know one thing through the law, and do another. For the good which I will, that I do not; but. Subject to sin, he does what he does not will. I do. I covet, not that the Apostle goes after concupiscence and it drags him to evil: he struggled, he was not subjugated: he sets this before you concerning himself, that you may not despair of it in yourself.
7.17: 7.17 Now then. Already redeemed: already having received the grace of Christ, he who before was sold under sin. Not I. The mind is free, the flesh captive. It dwells, though not consenting to it, he lives by faith. There are desires, but if they do not reign he himself does not do it, but would do it if he consented. But sin that dwells in me. How does it dwell, since it is not a substance but a privation of good? Behold, the body of the first man was corrupted by sin. And that corruption itself, through the condition of the offence, remains in the body, holding the strength of the divine sentence given in Adam, by whose fellowship the soul is stained with sin.
7.18: 7.18 For to will. To will not: because to will good is present with me, because it lies by the flesh and rests, powerless to rise to do good. Present: because it is in a manner natural to will good through reason, but such is this will that it is always overcome by the force of the flesh: but the will of God overcomes the flesh. To will. The things the law commands are good, so much so that he naturally loves them and wishes to do them, but the virtue of accomplishing is lacking. To will. AUG. The good man always wishes not to covet at all, but never accomplishes this in this life. To accomplish. He does not say to do, but to accomplish, because he does not do nothing. He does good: because he does not consent to concupiscence; but he does not accomplish that he should not covet at all, so also the enemy does evil, while he moves desire, but does not accomplish, because he does not draw to evil.
7.19: 7.19 For the good which I will. I find not how to accomplish good, because not even that good which I will. He shows it from the part from which it would seem less, but on the contrary evil, because even that which I will not, etc. Or, I find not good, because it is not there. For many fools do not find good in some thing, which nevertheless is there. AUG. It is one thing not to covet, another not to go after one's concupiscences. Not to covet is wholly of the perfect; not to go after one's concupiscences is of one fighting, of one wrestling. Where the fight is hot, why is victory despaired of?
7.20: 7.20 Now if, etc. He concludes the former sentence: therefore I do not work that, namely evil, from which the prior question is concluded, namely that he consents to the law of God. But sin that dwells in me. Pressed by sin, he does its will, which nevertheless is from the vice of man. He says this to note from how great things God rescues man.
7.21: 7.21 I find then. He had said the law good, nature good, which wills the same and consents to it: here he adds the good law as helper of good nature; and yet the outer man conquers those two joined: so that man, seeing he can escape by neither, is bound to grace. To me willing. Only: because I cannot accomplish, because evil is near to reason, lying in wait in the flesh as at the doors of the soul, and compels to do other than what man and the law will.
7.22: 7.22 According to the inner. AMBROSE. Because the flesh is derived from Adam it has sin in itself; if the soul were derived, sin would dwell in it also: because the soul of Adam sinned; but if the soul had sin in itself, man would not know himself.
7.23: 7.23 But I see. AUG. It belongs to the body of death that the law of the members fights against the law of the mind while the flesh lusts against the spirit. But the law of sin does not reign when its desires are not obeyed. A law in my members. Rightly is the fomes of sin called a law: because it was lawfully brought about that he who did not obey his superior should not have his inferior, that is the flesh, serve him. Captive. From the flesh, in part: because the mind resists, and delights with the law of God. So of the Apostle himself it is read: the mind does not consent to sin, death contends, the mind does not consent. There is in me something dead, something living: what is to be hoped from it?
7.24: 7.24 Unhappy. Not in mind, but in flesh. Who shall deliver me? He will be delivered when this mortal shall put on immortality, where no concupiscence shall remain.
7.25: 7.25 So then I myself. Here the third state, in the law of the spirit. But because he says that by grace he is freed, lest anyone grow sluggish, secure, as if sin would no longer harm, he determines how the deliverance is if he remains in grace. Otherwise sin will occupy him again. I myself. I in the flesh, I in the mind: not two, but one from both; with the mind I do not consent, with the flesh I covet.
8.1: 8.1 There is now therefore no. Even if before, not now: when in Christ. No condemnation. Because through the grace of baptism and the laver of regeneration the very guilt with which you were born is loosed, and whatever you committed before. AUG. Although they have desires of the flesh to which they do not consent, etc., up to but regeneration made this good.
8.2: 8.2 For the law of the spirit. Here he shows by what grace frees, namely by the Holy Spirit, because the law of the spirit. It is the Holy Spirit who teaches what is to be done and what not, who is the giver of life, and this through Christ who gives the Spirit: and how in Christ he explains.
8.3: 8.3 For what the law could not. He shows how the deliverance was made in Christ. Through the flesh. Through carnality, which rebelled, and, the law having been heard, was the more stirred up; thus the law of the letter was weakened through the flesh, and therefore it was impossible for it to free from the law of sin and death. Sending his own Son. AUG. Not where he was not: who is everywhere, etc., up to because he appeared visible to the world. In the likeness, etc. Not in sinful flesh; because not mother concupiscence but grace conceived him. He was not, then, a sinner, because he was neither conceived in the concupiscence of lust, nor had the cause of sin in himself, nor sinned in it. In punishment, then, he is like ours, not in the quality of sin. And of sin. ORIG. That is: Through the victim of his flesh which he offered on the altar of the cross, he condemned sin, and reduced it to nothing in his flesh. He condemned. That is, he destroyed the devil, that is, for the sin which he does in the flesh of Christ. Or he condemned sin, that is, the fomes proceeding from the sin of Adam, that is, weakened it.
8.4: 8.4 That the justification. Thus sin is condemned through Christ that the justice which the law of Moses promised might be fulfilled.
8.5: 8.5 For they that are according to the flesh. He who walks according to the flesh is not just, because neither is he who is according to it. Why not? because he desires carnal things as the highest goods, which is repugnant to justice.
8.6: 8.6 For the wisdom. He who savors these things which are of the flesh is not just; for the wisdom of the flesh is death. Life and peace. Life indeed in reference to that, the affection of the flesh is death; peace, however, in reference to what follows: the affection of the flesh is enmity against God.
8.7: 8.7 Because the wisdom of the flesh. By enumerating these things he deters from obedience to the flesh. Is an enemy. While it thinks God can do nothing beyond what is seen in the natures of things.
8.9: 8.9 Yet if. He speaks doubtfully, because they are not yet of perfect faith, but there is hope of perfecting. The Spirit of God. The Spirit of Christ, because the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ is the same.
8.10: 8.10 The body indeed. By the name of body he signifies the whole man, as Ezechiel conversely by the name of soul, when he says: The soul that sins, etc. And the sense is: If the Spirit of Christ is in you, although the body be dead, that is, the man be dead on account of sins, that is in sins, yet the spirit, that is the soul which had been ungodly, lives: because it is joined to God, who is life, and this on account of justification, that is, the remission of sins, which is from the Holy Spirit.
