Dead, he says, not mortal. For before sin the body was animal, that is mortal, namely able to die. But that it was not necessary to die: now it is called dead on account of sin, that is that it is necessary to die. For sin to be avoided, this infirmity is reserved, that thenceforth he may fear to sin the more.
8.11: 8.11 And if the Spirit. AUG. Attend that the Holy Spirit, etc., up to as also the generation of the Son who shall declare? Shall quicken also your mortal bodies. THE SAME. Behold the fourth state. In the first action, etc., up to because we had deserted God who is above us. Mortal. Not dead, because in the resurrection, when this mortal shall put on immortality, not only the necessity of dying, which it now has on account of sin, but not even the mortality which the animal body had before sin will remain. Because of his Spirit that dwells. It appears most evidently that man deserved, on account of sin, death not only of the Spirit but also of the body, and that through the Holy Spirit both were freed by Christ.
8.13: 8.13 But if by the Spirit. Either the Holy Spirit or our own spirit: which, however, is only so when the Holy Spirit is acting.
8.14: 8.14 Are led. He says they are led, not ruled. For to be led is more than to be ruled: for we say someone is led as one who is scarcely doing anything himself, but ruled as one already doing something, who is ruled so that he may act rightly. But they are led, not because they do nothing of themselves, but because, in order to do something, they are driven by the impulse of grace. AUG., book On Rebuke and Grace, ch. 2. Let them not therefore deceive themselves who say: Why should we, etc., up to let them rejoice that they have received.
8.15: 8.15 For you have not received, etc. You ought to be sons, not slaves, because you have not received the spirit of bondage, which makes people serve unwillingly through fear of punishment. But you have received the spirit of adoption. It is the same Spirit, but because of its different works it is called by different names: it is called the spirit of wrath for the Egyptians, to whom the water divided by the Spirit did harm. It is not called the spirit of wrath for the sons of Israel, to whom the divided water was of benefit. It is the spirit of fear for those who, convicted by the law of their sins and their own weakness, did not understand the grace of the Spirit. It is the spirit of liberty, by his work, for those to whom regeneration unto eternal life and the faith which works through love have been imparted. There is therefore one Spirit who makes two fears. And they also make two kinds of servants. For there is a servant who is also a son, who fears the Lord and honors his father; hence Malachias: If I am the Lord, where is my fear? If I am a father, where is my honor? Malach. 1. And there is a servant who fears punishment but does not love justice. And since mention is made of fears, it should be known that, apart from the natural fear which is in all, there are four fears, namely: worldly fear, which is evil and not from God; servile fear, which is good and from God but is not sufficient; initial fear, which is good and sufficient; and chaste fear, which is good and perfecting, of which he speaks here: For he himself begets us as sons of God. In whom we cry. This again is from the gift of the Spirit, who makes us cry Abba, in Hebrew, father in Latin. Abba, Father. The Apostle put both on account of the sacrament. And in the passion Christ said, Abba, Father, because the Church is made of both peoples; having compassion on her, he showed in himself that her sons (namely the martyrs) ought not to despair if at any time in the passion some sadness creeps in from human frailty.
8.16: 8.16 That we are the sons of God. The Holy Spirit makes us recognize this, while the remission of sins takes place in the Church; and although the whole Trinity does this, it is nevertheless understood to belong to the Holy Spirit, because he is common to the Father and the Son, and is the union of both; through him fellowship and unity come about, by which we are made one body of the only Son of God. For unity binds us together, and charity makes it, and charity is only from the Holy Spirit. These things are said so that we may love unity and fear separation.
8.17: 8.17 Heirs. Although God does not die, as is said under human laws. Or he will die, so that he may not be seen through a mirror in an enigma as now, but face to face. It can also be said that Christ our head, departing to his passion, left us the possession of ecclesiastical peace, as he himself says: My peace I give to you, my peace I leave to you Joan. 14. Christ also is our inheritance. Hence: The Lord is the portion of my inheritance Psal. 15., etc. If however we suffer with him. No one can mortify the deeds of the flesh, from which life will come, without hardship, for which patience is necessary.
8.19: 8.19 For the expectation of the creature. The creature means the good, who remain in the creation of God, or because they are the cause of all. Corruption is the vanity to which the creature is subject. For all things that are born are weak and corruptible, and by this vain: because they cannot hold their own state. AUG. As for what he says, for the expectation, etc. It must be so understood that neither the sense, etc., up to labors and is subject to corruption.
8.20: 8.20 Not willingly, etc. It sinned willingly, but does not bear the punishment willingly, in that it is subjected to deceit: but this is because of the justice and clemency of him who both punishes sin and intends to heal.
8.21: 8.21 Because the creature also itself. AUG. For now it is only creature, while the form of the sons is not yet perfect, etc., up to for man, having lost the seal of the image, remained only creature. Shall be delivered. It will be revealed; it awaits the revelation; he subjected; it will be delivered. All these things through the Spirit.
8.22: 8.22 Every creature. AUG. Man. Every creature is either corporeal, etc., up to even if not in all men. Every creature. AMBR. All the elements fulfill their duties with labor, which is for our sake: hence they will rest when we are taken up; and therefore let us prepare ourselves diligently. Groans. It is always new in this, which is indicated by the inchoative verb, and for the desire of the heavenly homeland. Travails. That is, it grieves. Even until now. AUG. Because even if someone has ceased to grieve in the bosom of Abraham, nevertheless until now, in those who are not yet freed, every creature groans.
8.23: 8.23 Not only, etc. AUG. That is, not only in man of the body, but we also in ourselves apart from the body, apart from the troubles of the body. Not only. AUG., in the Exposition of propositions, the 53rd, on the Epistle to the Romans. Not only that which is called creature alone in men, etc., up to or by troubling hardship. The firstfruits of the spirit. That is, those whose spirits have already been offered to God as a sacrifice, and kindled with the divine fire of charity. Adoption. So that the body also may receive the benefit of adoption, and they may be sons of God in every part.
8.24: 8.24 For by hope. He says this so that the merit of hope may seem greater and therefore it ought to save. The Spirit helps our infirmity. AUG. Because we groan and ask to be freed, but lest we ask either before the time or in a contrary way, the Spirit helps. That prayer obtains is plainly a gift of God, but even to pray is of grace.
8.26: 8.26 Unspeakable. For how could it be spoken, when what is unknown is desired? Yet it is not altogether unknown. For if it were wholly unknown, it would not be desired. And again, if it were seen, it would not be sought with groanings. He searches. AMBR. Not as though seeking what he does not know, from whom nothing is hidden, and to whom the prayer of all spirits is known.
8.28: 8.28 And we know that to them that love, etc. As if he said: Not only does the Holy Spirit do this, but he also makes all things turn out for good to those who love him, whether prosperous or adverse; for such a God consoles in prosperity and exercises in adversity. The evils, therefore, which the faithful piously endure are profitable, either for amending or removing sins, or for exercising and proving justice, or for showing the misery of this life. For although the death of the flesh came originally from the sin of the first man, nevertheless its good use made the most glorious martyrs. And therefore not only death itself, but also all the evils of the world had to remain once sins were forgiven, so that man might have things with which to struggle for the truth, and by which the virtue of the faithful might be exercised. According to his purpose. As if he said: That they have been called is from nothing other than the predestination of God. And hence it is that all things work together for good: not from merit.
8.29: 8.29 For whom, God, he predestined, that is, he prepared by added grace to believe the word of preaching: those he foreknew, that is, knew long before, to be made conformable to the Son, who is the image of the Father, in every way the same as the Father. Hence it is said: He that sees me sees the Father also Joan. 14. Of the image. That we may bear the image of the heavenly one, as we have borne the image of the earthly. Or firstborn. Because before every creature he was not made but born, and because he was the first born without sin, and the first to rise impassible, in whom he has brothers.
8.30: 8.30 He called. The exterior calling takes place through preachers and is common to the good and the wicked. But the interior calling is only for the elect. Of the exterior it is said: Many are called, but few are chosen. Predestination is fulfilled by the calling. To call is to aid the knowledge of faith or to prick the heart of the one whom he makes hear, and this is only of the elect. He glorified. This is said of those foreknown; not of others, who even if they believe for a time and seem good, are not glorified because they do not persevere. He glorified, or will glorify: this is in fact future, but is said in the past tense, because God is said to have done what he disposed from eternity to do; hence Isaias: Who made the things that are to come Isa. 44. For such as these all things work for good, even their straying, so that they may thereby be more cautious and not trust in themselves. Four things are mentioned here: predestination, calling, justification, glorification. One is in God, and three in us. For our predestination is not in us, but hidden with him in his foreknowledge. But the other three are in us.
8.31: 8.31 If God is for us. AUG. God is for us in that he predestined us before we existed, called us when we were turned away, justified us when we were sinners, and will glorify us when we are mortal.
8.32: 8.32 He delivered up. This is said because the Father delivered up the Son, yet the author of this chalice is also he himself who drinks it. Hence the Apostle: Christ loved us, and delivered himself up for us Ephes. 5. If then the Father delivered up the Son, and the Son delivered up himself, what did Judas do? The Father, by delivering up the Son, did well; the Son, by delivering up himself, did well; Judas, by delivering up his master out of avarice, did evil. For what has been granted to us from the passion of Christ will not be credited to the malice of Judas; he will have the reward of malice, Christ the praise of grace. All things. It is less to give us all things than to deliver Christ to death for our sake. And so all things above, namely God the Trinity, are ours to see and enjoy. Things equal, namely the angels, to whom we shall be made equal in the future, to live with them, though now we are lower. Lower things also are ours for dominion. And likewise some higher things also, such as the sublime angels, and all the heavenly ministries of God, are ours, not by dominion but by use; just as the things of the master belong to the servants, for sustenance, namely, or ornament or something of the kind.
8.34: 8.34 At the right hand of God. In the honor in which God is, whose petition cannot be despised. He makes intercession. While daily he offers to the Father's countenance the man whom he assumed, and the grievous kind of death which he endured for us.
8.35: 8.35 Who then shall separate us, etc. CYPR. None of these things can separate believers, etc., up to that we also may suffer for his sake: But in all these things we overcome.
8.38: 8.38 Neither angels, nor principalities, nor virtues. These orders are understood of the evil angels, and of the good if it could be.
8.39: 8.39 Nor height, nor depth. That is, neither prosperity nor adversity; hence Solomon: Give me neither riches nor poverty: lest being filled I be tempted to deny, or being compelled by poverty I steal, and forswear the name of my God Prov. 30. Many sin by height, many by necessity. Against this is set Achaz in Isaias, who would not ask a sign either in the height or in the depth. The remedy is from Christ, who was neither lifted up by the power by which he is equal to the Father, nor disturbed by the casting out of death, who is the sign in the height and in the depth: so that he was neither exalted by royal power nor disturbed by distress, as was then the case on account of the war of the Assyrians.
9.1: 9.1 I speak the truth. Now nothing can separate me, but once I was separated; hence now I grieve, and so the evils are now turned into good. I speak the truth. AMBR. Because he seemed to speak against the Jews, etc., up to yet Job was the fifth from Abraham among the sons of Esau, that is, the grandson of Esau.
9.3: 9.3 For my brethren. The Jews, or also for those to be drawn back who are now brothers in faith, who are also my kinsmen: and so I sinned the more gravely. AUG. Such perfect eminence of the Son is declared here, etc., up to: The mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus I Tim. 2.
9.6: 9.6 Not that the word of God hath miscarried. The Apostle consoles his sorrow. For who would lament one who had long been held as dead? God, foreknowing, did not decree long ago that these should be saved, being no respecter of persons. For he condemns no one before he sins, crowns no one before he conquers; but by foreknowledge he has determined what the will of each will be, from which he is condemned or crowned. Because he grieved over the Jews, he consoles himself, finding it written that not all are to be saved, but only those like Isaac. In these he shows that the grace of God alone will make sons of God. Not that the word of God hath miscarried. From his having said that the promise of the eternal inheritance was made to the Jews, who themselves in great part did not believe, the word of God seemed not to have been fulfilled. To this he answers: Even if it was not fulfilled in some, yet it was fulfilled in others, namely in the believing Gentiles, who are now the true sons of Abraham. Not that it hath miscarried. As if he said: Even if he has labored thus; even if not all believe, yet the word of God has not miscarried; or, I do not say that it has miscarried. For the word of God to miscarry is for the promises not to be fulfilled.
9.7: 9.7 In Isaac. That is, in Christ, by the calling of grace, they are gathered. In the promise to Isaac were prefigured, not those who make themselves just, but those whom God makes; these are the sons of the free woman who is above, who is our mother. The sons of the flesh are of the earthly Jerusalem, which is in bondage with her children. Just as Isaac did not merit to be promised before his birth, so too these; but the adoption of sons was promised and given to them by grace alone.
9.10: 9.10 And not only she. Sara had a promise, but Rebecca also had a promise, having two sons by one act of intercourse of Isaac our father. He says by one act, lest the merits of the parents seem to make a difference in the offspring; but of the father, that is, of our founder, whom we should imitate if we wish to be sons of God. The promise made to Sara shows that no one is saved because of lineage. But this promise made to Rebecca shows that no one is chosen because of any merit of his own or of his parents, but by grace alone.
9.11: 9.11 For when they were not yet born. Rebecca had this promise: The elder shall serve the younger, that is, Esau, by persecuting Jacob, will benefit him.
9.12: 9.12 Not of works. Future ones, which would not have been good or evil without grace added or withdrawn. AUG. But if it is said that the divine judgment distinguished their future conduct, etc., up to for how are those things called future which will not exist?
9.13: 9.13 The elder shall serve the younger. This is literal: because the Idumeans, who descended from Esau (who is also called Edom), were subject to the sons of Israel; but this prophecy looks more to the fact that the people of the Jews, the elder, that is, earlier in the worship of the one God, would serve the younger, that is, the later Christian people. Jacob I have loved, etc. In Jacob he found nothing to love but the gift of his own mercy. In Esau he hates nothing but original sin. But how is this right, when they had done nothing? Because the matter is astonishing, he raises the objection against himself: What shall we say then? It is of mercy to will and to run; which appears in others of the same mass, for whom perdition is due.
9.14: 9.14 What shall we say then? Because he chose this one and rejected that one without merit, will God be called unjust? No, because he chose the one by mercy and rejected the other by justice. In neither is there iniquity; the one by mercy, because Moses says so; the other by justice, because Scripture says so, introducing God speaking to Pharao. God forbid. It is established that no one is freed except by free mercy; no one is condemned except by most equitable justice. But why he frees this one rather than that one, let him search who can so deep a judgment; yet let him beware of the precipice.
9.15: 9.15 I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy. That is, on whom I foreknow that mercy is to be shown, and who will remain with me: this is to give to him to whom it is to be given, not to give to him to whom it is not to be given; so that he calls the one whom he knows will obey; as David, who after pardon persevered so well. Saul, not heard in his prayer, did not persevere, but turned to idols; hence he seems justly to have been rejected by the one who foreknew.
9.16: 9.16 So then it is not of him that willeth, etc. As if he said: The will of man alone is not enough, if there is not also the mercy of God. To which it is said in reply: The mercy of God is not enough either, if there is not the will of man; and by this, if that was rightly said, why is it not also rightly said on the contrary: It is not of God that hath mercy, but of man that willeth? It remains, then, that what was said be understood rightly in this way: that the whole be given to God, who both prepares the good will of man to be helped, and helps it when prepared: he goes before the one willing that he may will, and follows the one willing that he may not will in vain. AUG. Who, moreover, is so impiously foolish as to say that God does not turn the evil wills of men, etc., up to just as from his mercy he bestows grace.
9.17: 9.17 I have raised thee up. Or I have stirred thee up, or I have preserved thee. AMBR. For this very thing I have preserved thee, etc., up to but that, thee being hardened, I may show my power by the signs of Egypt.
9.18: 9.18 Therefore he hath mercy on whom he will. There is no merit of mercy; the merit of hardening is the sin of the whole condemned mass. Nor does he harden by imparting malice, but by not imparting mercy, as they are not worthy, which he does by a hidden equity, remote from human senses, because the Apostle does not explain it but marvels: O the depth of the riches. He hardeneth. AUG., epist. 105. Not as though he compels anyone to sin, but only because he does not bestow the mercy of his justification on certain sinners, for this reason he is said to harden them, because he has no mercy on them, not because he drives them to sin. And he has no mercy on those to whom he judges, by a most hidden equity, remote from human senses, that grace is not to be given.
9.19: 9.19 Why doth he then find fault? Since it is established that it is from the will of God, why is it asked how one is good and another is evil? There is no need, because each will be such as God wills him to be, and therefore he unjustly condemns one and saves another: or, why is there complaint, that is, why does anyone strive to act well, since he can do nothing except what God wills?
9.20: 9.20 O man. This is not from lack of a reason to give, but he calls man back to himself.
9.21: 9.21 Of the same lump. So the whole mass of the human race is justly corrupt and muddy: if from it a vessel is made unto honor, it is mercy; if unto dishonor, it is just, because this was from nature: behold justice in those who have no time for working; but about those who have time he adds: what if God willing, namely, what would you answer to God. Another unto dishonor. A vessel unto honor, but unto dishonor: if it is base, it has clay from itself, not from the potter. What if God, etc. AUG., book 1, to Simplicianus, question 2. As if he said: It has already been shown that even if God gives nothing good, he is not unjust, etc., up to but they have abused this grace.
9.22: 9.22 Endured. God endures the wicked in order to destroy them in an orderly way; and he uses them as an instrument for the salvation of the good. For God would not create any of the angels or men whom he foreknew would be evil, unless he likewise knew for what good uses he would employ them.
9.23: 9.23 That he might shew. As if he said: For this he suffers the wicked, and shows his wrath beforehand, and draws them to the knowledge of himself, that he might show on the vessels of mercy, that is, on the elect through mercy, the riches of glory, that is, how rich and how great and glorious his mercy is; for this reason he gives so many goods to the wicked, to convict them that they are justly condemned, so that the faithful may love him the more, for whom he has preserved that same grace.
9.25: 9.25 As in Osee. Since it has been shown that they are sons by grace alone, he begins to prove through the prophets that these are of both peoples.
9.27: 9.27 If the number. Behold, the salvation of the Jews is spoken of in such a way that the greater part is blinded.
9.28: 9.28 For a consummating word. The prophet adds through what they are saved, namely through the word of the Gospel, so that the glory of the works of the law may be excluded. For the word of the Gospel, which is called consummating, leads to perfection and abridges all the legal things in the one Christ: yet it is equal to the earlier word of the law; hence is added, in equity, that is, so that nothing be lacking to justice of all the things prefigured, or because it retains the things that are equitable, such as the moral precepts, and cuts off the things that it is right to remove, such as the figures. And a short word in equity. So that by the compendium of faith he saves by grace, not by countless observances. And lest anyone doubt, the Prophet adds: Unless the Lord of Sabaoth. The Lord made the word, which was so necessary, that unless there were seed, that is, the word, etc. Or by the seed are understood the remnant to be saved, that is, the apostles and other good people, and unless the word of God had been preached through them, the Gentiles would have perished. And this is: Unless the Lord of hosts, when he blinded others, had left us, that is, for our benefit, a seed, that is, the apostles, from whom the harvest of Christ grew. And we had been made like Gomorrha. He put both, to note the likeness of guilt and punishment, as if to say: We would have been equal in punishment, because we would have been alike in guilt.
9.31: 9.31 Israel. But Israel followed the law as if backward, because he never attains the spiritual understanding. Following after the law of justice. The law of Moses is the law of justice, if it is well understood. Or, following the justice of the law, that is, that which is from fear of punishment, not from love of justice, he has not attained, etc.
9.32: 9.32 Because not by faith. For he did not seek to be justified by faith, and because he did not ask justice from God, he did not believe in him who justifies the ungodly, not believing that God works in man that he may be justified. Whence it happened that they did not believe, he supplies. They stumbled. Like a small stone which one does not guard against, Christ was fit to cause stumbling, hidden in humility. Isaias bears witness to this, ch. 8. Behold I lay, that is, I cause to be born, in Sion, that is, among the Jews, Christ, a stone of stumbling, which, being small, is not guarded against, and a rock of scandal, that is, utterly crushing the wicked in the future, and grieving them. Christ is called a stone of stumbling according to the state in which he appeared here to the wicked. But a rock of scandal according to what he will do to the wicked in the future.
9.33: 9.33 And a rock of scandal. It is called a rock before polishing and a stone after polishing. The polishing of Christ was the passion, in which he laid aside the misery of infirmity. Therefore Christ before the passion was a rock of scandal, at which time the Jews were scandalized, angry and indignant that he made himself the Son of God. He was a stone by polishing, Christ in the passion, when the same Jews especially stumbled and were blinded, not believing him to be God whom they saw dead. He shall not be confounded. AUG. For he who believes in him will not have his own justice, which is from the law, though the law is good, but will fulfill the law itself, not by his own justice, but by one given by God. For thus he shall not be confounded.
10.1: 10.1 And prayer. For the will, to be moved to believe true things, is not sufficient for itself unless God helps it by grace; hence: No man cometh to me, unless it be given him by my Father Joan. 4.
10.2: 10.2 For I bear them witness that. AMBR. He speaks of those who did not receive Christ not out of envy but out of error; to whom Peter says: I know that you did it through ignorance Act. 3. Not according to knowledge. For it is foolish to venerate the law and persecute the God of the law.
10.3: 10.3 For they, not knowing the justice of God. Not that by which God is just, but that which is in man from God. They have not submitted to the justice of God. This is the justice of God, which is established not in the precept of the law by which fear is instilled, but in the help of the grace of Christ.
10.4: 10.4 The end. Not consuming but perfecting: he therefore perfects justice through faith without the works of the law. Christ. Justice is from Christ; for if it were through the written or natural law, and not by the faith of Christ, then Christ died in vain. Unto justice. Not human but divine. For there is human and divine: of the human, there, Moses; of the divine, there: But that which is of, etc. Scripture. In Numbers and Leviticus it is thus: He that shall do those things shall live in them.
10.5: 10.5 Shall live in it. He has this reward, namely, that he is not punished by this death. But it is not great justice to fear, nor does it have merit with God.
10.6: 10.6 That is, to bring Christ down. That is, to deny that Christ ascended.
10.8: 10.8 The word is nigh. That is, it is useful, or it is not something unfitting either to say or to believe. Or nigh, because it is not far from the nature of souls: and in the manner of speaking, because it is said to us that we may believe. This is the word. AUG., Tract. 80, on John. Of which the Lord said: Now you are clean by reason of the word which I have spoken to you, etc., up to for even in the word itself one thing is the passing sound, another the abiding power.
10.9: 10.9 Because if thou confess. AUG. Behold the praise of faith and its reward. The praise of faith is, if you believe that Jesus is Lord, etc., up to which precedes it in the resurrection fitting to itself, that is, in justification.
10.10: 10.10 With the heart we believe. The rest one can do unwillingly, but one cannot believe unless willingly. Confession. AUG., on Psalm 30, discourse 3. To confess is to say what is in the heart, etc., up to because as he believes, so he ought also with the mouth, so that he may thus preach.
10.12: 10.12 That call upon him. One who prays calls upon; but this surely cannot be unless he first believes. Those therefore who call upon him not only believe but also pray, so that after someone's mind has believed, it does not cease to ask for what God promised to those who watch with the whole heart, because to believe gives remission of sins. But to call upon obtains the promises of God.
10.14: 10.14 How then shall they call on him, etc. Having proved that it is taken from both peoples, he shows through what, namely through the mission made to both, which whoever has not received is inexcusable. Calling upon saves, therefore it is necessary to believe: because, how, etc. Or how shall they believe, etc. As if he said: They will not believe unless they hear. For no one ever believed who did not hear in some way, either inwardly or outwardly. He says that to believe is from hearing, hearing from preaching, preaching from the sending of God; so that the whole descends from the fountain of grace. And preaching is truly from sending, because God also sent even false teachers announcing well, he who knows how to use the wicked for good. Sometimes also he sends the wicked to the wicked in wrath, that is, he permits the wicked to preach to the wicked for their punishment, that in turn they may perish through themselves, as is just. AUG. As for the Apostle's saying: How shall they believe him of whom they have not heard? He said this of the Gentiles, etc., up to that the preachers of Christ were to be sent.
10.15: 10.15 And how shall they preach unless they be sent? Behold, it appears that preachers were sent to the Gentiles also. How beautiful. Because they enlighten the world, in which it appears that they are sent by God; otherwise they could not do this. Peace. Reconciliation between people and people, the partition wall of the legal rite among the Jews and of idolatry among the Gentiles having been broken down. And between God and the ungodly through justifying faith, and men who believe in him. Of them that bring glad tidings of good things. Peace upon peace, because the kingdom of God too is peace.
10.16: 10.16 For Isaias saith, etc. God foreknowing foretold the unbelief of the Jews, but did not cause it; nor would he have foreknown their evils unless they had them. So also he blinds by forsaking, not by making, and the will merited this. If it is said that the Jews cannot believe because Isaias foretold it, I say they cannot because they will not. What God foreknew, he foretold; but he did not make it. They cannot, while proud, while such that they attribute everything to their own strength and deny that divine help is necessary for them to act well.
10.17: 10.17 Faith then cometh by, etc. Although God teaches within, still the herald announces outwardly. By the word. That is, by the grace of Christ who sends us the teachers of the evangelical word. For unless something is said, it can neither be heard nor believed.
10.18: 10.18 But I say. Or rather, that is, certainly, and thus they are inexcusable, as David shows in the Psalms, saying: Their sound hath gone forth into all the earth. AUG., epist. 80, which is to Hesychius. It was not fulfilled at this time of the Apostles, etc., up to so also that: You shall be witnesses to me even to the uttermost part of the earth Act. 1.
10.19: 10.19 But I say: Hath not Israel. He proved that all heard, and so that the Jews heard. But because they might have heard and not known, he affirms that they also knew. Hath known. Israel is said to have known the doctrine of the Gospel and the coming of Christ, because he could not contradict by reason or authority; but he did not truly know, so as to sit well in their mind. To jealousy. It is envy for the Jews when the Gentiles call their God their own, and say that the promises and their law and the prophets pertain to them. By that which is not a nation. The Gentiles were not formerly called a holy nation, because they were without the law; or now not a nation, because they do not live as Gentiles. By a foolish nation. By, that is, against a foolish nation, that is, against the Gentiles who did not know the true God.
10.21: 10.21 All the day long. During all the time in which I dwelt with them, and enlightened the world, I abundantly showed the Jews my works and affection; or in a part of the whole day, on the cross I stretched forth my hands, etc. I have stretched forth my hands. As if he said: I showed greater things to the Jews. For he denied them no benefit; for he raised their dead, he cured their various infirmities. And he is said to stretch forth his hands who generously bestows benefits on those who ask.
11.2: 11.2 Foreknew. For predestined, he put foreknew. For so it should be taken, as is clear from what follows; and he said foreknew so that the Jews might not again become proud from his having said that they were not rejected, and the people of God. AUG. Will anyone dare to say that God did not foreknow to whom he would give the gift of believing, or whom he would give to his Son so that he would lose none of them? If he foreknew these, he surely foreknew his benefits by which he deigns to free us. This predestination of the saints is nothing other than the foreknowledge, and the preparation, of the benefits of God by which most certainly all who are freed are freed. Know you not. As if he said: So the Lord has not rejected the remnant at this time, but has saved them; as in the time of Elias he reserved many for himself, when Elias alone seemed to himself to remain, and if he did not know that others besides himself were reserved, it is no wonder if these are ignorant.
11.4: 11.4 Seven thousand. By the number seven, universality is signified; by the thousand, perfection.
11.5: 11.5 Even so then. As if he said: There were then many, though Elias did not know. Even so, that is, thus hiddenly; or even so, that is, by the same grace.
11.6: 11.6 Otherwise grace is no more grace. That is, if they were saved otherwise (which cannot be done except by the grace of God), then grace itself will no longer be grace, but a debt.
11.7: 11.7 What then? Having heard that the remnant were saved by grace and not of works, what then must be said? But the election hath obtained it. Election is of grace, not of merits. But blinding is of merits. For they were blinded because they would not believe, just as those believed because they willed. Mercy and judgment, therefore, were wrought by God in their very wills, by his adding grace to some through mercy, and permitting the others to be blinded by judgment. For whoever, having understood, refused to believe, ought to obtain what he wishes, namely that henceforth he cannot believe. They were helped, therefore, in their own will, not by malice being put in, but by grace being withdrawn; so that, because knowing the truth they said it was false, they would henceforth not understand what is true. The envy of an evil will deserves this; it is not so with those who do this through error.
11.8: 11.8 God hath given them the spirit of remorse. This signifies a bad remorse, because it often happens that even what is good is irksome to a man, as the doctrine of Christ was to the Pharisees; and so he calls the spirit of remorse the envious mind with which they envied the doctrine of Christ. Until this present day. That is, as long as it can be called today, that is, until the present day of all to whom this writing shall come.
11.9: 11.9 Table. That is, Scripture: theirs, that is, which was first offered to them, and set before them, because they delight in its carnal observances; or, before them, because if they wished to attend to reason, they could understand. For a snare, etc. As they themselves offered me vinegar, so let iniquity be a snare to them, because they knew iniquity and persisted in it. For a snare, etc. Scripture, which is bread to those who understand, ensnares when it is wrongly understood and the preaching of Christ is rejected on account of it. Likewise the Scripture of the law was the cause of captivity, since in zeal for it they killed Christ, and in that captivity it was the cause of scandal and reproach to them, and afterward will be the cause of eternal damnation, which is specially called the retribution of God.
11.10: 11.10 Let their eyes be darkened. Because they saw not without cause, let it be to them not to see. Let their eyes be darkened. These words are said not by the wish of one desiring, but by the office of one foretelling.
11.11: 11.11 I say then, Have they. Because I say they were blinded by the authority of the prophets, do you think they fell irrecoverably and without benefit? As if he said, no. But their fall is profitable, and they can be restored, so that no one should despise them. Have they so stumbled that they should fall? AUG. He does not say this because they did not fall, etc., up to but rather let them beware lest, while they are proud, they fall. Salvation. While scattered through the world they are a testimony that the prophecies about Christ are not fictions. That they may be jealous of them. It can be taken thus: that the Jews may imitate the Gentiles in good. This has often happened, and will happen more fully at the end of the world, when the Jews follow the Christians at the end of Christ. For then the hand of Moses will be drawn back into his bosom, then our Moses will return to the mother and to the brothers. It can also be understood that the Gentiles may be jealous of the Jews, that is, may believe as they themselves once believed. As though the Gentiles were moved by emulation of God regarding the evil works of the Jews.
11.12: 11.12 Now if, etc. As if he said: I said that the offence of the Jews is profitable; if that is so, then their conversion will profit much more. How much more. That is, if God turns their evil into good, that is, into the riches of the world, much more their good, when at the end their fullness, converted, will enrich the Gentiles by doctrine and example. In this he shows that their fall is neither useless nor irrecoverable.
11.13: 11.13 As long as. ANSELM. Although I am the apostle of the Gentiles, yet I will honor my ministry by adding beyond what I owe, so as to labor also for the Jews, making the attempt; if this way does not succeed, I will try another, which I would not do if I despaired of their salvation. CHRYS. Again he strives to free himself from an evil suspicion. He seems indeed to rebuke those who were of the Gentiles and to humble their minds; yet gradually he pricks the Jew.
11.16: 11.16 For if the firstfruit. I said that their taking up will be very profitable; and lest you say that the Gentiles cannot be made so, as though the whole race were repudiated, I say that if the firstfruit, that is, a few of them taken up, as the apostles and other disciples, is holy. And the lump. That is, the race can be sanctified. And if the root. That is, the patriarchs, from whom the saints draw the sap of faith. And the branches. Who have grown out of their race, grounded in their faith.
11.17: 11.17 Being a wild olive, art grafted in, etc. ANSELM. Let us see how the Lord himself foretells the grafting in of the wild olive and the breaking off of the branches, etc., up to what the Lord foretold would be done. Partaker. In the hope of the promise: this is against custom. For a good tree is usually grafted into one that is not good; here a not good one into a good one.
11.18: 11.18 Boast not, etc. ANSELM. The Gentiles, already believing in Christ, were lifting themselves up against the Jews, because they had crucified Christ, though from them also came another wall to the cornerstone, and therefore the Apostle restrains them. Boast not, he says, etc., that is, you are not stable if you destroy those through whom you stand.
11.19: 11.19 Thou wilt say then: The branches were broken off. As if he said: If not against those who stand, yet it is permitted to boast against those who were cast off for the cause of my grafting in; which the Apostle removes thus: You say well, because it is true that they were broken off because of unbelief; you stand by faith, that is, not by your merit but by the grace of God; and therefore be not proud, lest you also be broken off through pride, as they through unbelief. You are not stable if you destroy those through whom you stand. He is easily deceived who rejoices in the evils of others.
11.20: 11.20 Thou standest by faith. That you stand is a benefit of God, not your merit. But fear. Lest you lose the benefit of so great a grace, and fall into punishment. For fear is chaste when the soul is careful lest God, forsaken, forsake it.
11.22: 11.22 If thou abide in goodness. If you have acted worthily of the kindness of God, for you do not need faith alone. The severity of God. That he did not spare them, because he found them unworthy of the virtue of their fathers.
11.24: 11.24 Contrary to nature. That is called contrary to nature which is contrary to the custom of nature, as if a graft were to bear the fruit of the root. God, however, does nothing contrary to nature, because what he does is nature. The olive. By the olive is here understood the faith of the Fathers.
11.25: 11.25 For I would not have you ignorant, etc. AUG. The defenders of the law, the handlers of the law, the teachers of the law, the interpreters of the law, crucified the author of the law. O blindness! This is that which has fallen in part on Israel, that Christ might be crucified, and the fullness of the Gentiles might come in.
11.26: 11.26 Ungodliness. That is, unbelief, or the cult of legal observance. For the worship of the Jews, from the coming of Christ being known, is ungodliness.
11.27: 11.27 I shall take away. This will be at the end, when the Jews will be converted by the preaching of Elias and Enoch; hence through Malachias: I will send you Elias the Thesbite, who shall turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the hearts of the children to the father Mal. 4.; so that the sons may understand as the fathers, that is, as the prophets understood.
11.28: 11.28 AUG. According to the Gospel, etc. Or thus: then they would be converted; but now they are enemies indeed of Christ, and indeed of ours. Again from themselves, namely from their own vice. But this is according to the Gospel and for your sakes, that is, for the progress of the Gospel and of you. Enemies for. He shows that this comes from the disposition of God. For of themselves they can be enemies, which benefits the Gospel, God using evils for good, so that when they act against the will of God, the will of God, wisely disposing all things, is fulfilled. For the sake of the fathers. The elect are beloved for the sake of the fathers, to whom these things were promised; because they were not called by that calling by which many not foreknown are called who nevertheless perish, of which it was said: Many are called, but few are chosen Marc. 20.; but by that by which the elect are called, which is without change: because he who hears from the Father comes to the Son, who loses nothing of all that is given; but whoever perishes was not of that number; hence: They went out from us, but they were not of us I Joan. 2. According to election and for the sake of the fathers. Aug., book On the Predestination of the Saints, ch. 16. They are to be saved: because the gifts, that is, the promises, etc., up to because they do not see them with sorrow.
11.30: 11.30 For as. That is, for the reason that God once permitted you not to believe, namely lest, converted afterward, you should have cause for pride.
11.31: 11.31 That they also. Having experienced that salvation is not through the law but through grace: so that thus through humility they may obtain mercy.
11.32: 11.32 Hath concluded. That is, has permitted to be concluded. Here he seems in some way to expound the mystery. For God concluded all in unbelief, so that, confounded by repentance for the bitterness of their unbelief, and converted by believing to the sweetness of the mercy of God, they might remain more humble, so that the grace of the gift might be most welcome, and they might cry out: How great is the multitude of thy sweetness, O Lord Psal. 30. Of all. That is, of the Jews and Gentiles, not that he will condemn no one, as some have falsely supposed.
11.33: 11.33 O the depth, etc. He had put forward a statement of marvelous profundity, and as if struck with awe at its profundity he exclaims, O the depth, etc. For we have a very small understanding for examining the justice of the judgments of God, for examining the free grace given with no preceding merits. Nor does it move us so much that grace is granted to the unworthy, as that it is denied to others equally unworthy. AUG., book On the Spirit and the Letter, ch. 36 at the end. I know that, as there is no impossibility, so there is no iniquity with God, etc., up to that he first permitted them to be concluded in unbelief. THE SAME. Sometimes the grace of God is granted to the children of unbelievers, etc., up to and if not in this life, certainly in the other, etc. His ways. That is, the fulfillments of his disposition, because even in the carrying out it cannot be known what he disposed. Counsellor. The counsellor of the Father is his only-begotten Son, who is also called the Angel of great counsel. But of men and angels none was his counsellor.
11.35: 11.35 Or who hath first. Even if we cannot know the judgments of God, at least this is certain, that he gives goods from grace alone, and not from preceding merit. AUG. God has become a debtor, not by receiving anything from us, etc., up to and you have done this, you who helped those who labor, etc.
11.36: 11.36 For of him, etc. Of, by, in, indicate the distinction of persons; but he, the same pronoun repeated, indicates identity of substance; and because such glory is for him, not for the just themselves. AUG., book On the Nature of the Good, ch. 27. Of him. Not from him are all things, etc., up to he wished each of these three to be referred to each person. All things. When we hear that all things are of God, we must understand all natures, and all things that exist naturally; for sins, which vitiate nature, are not of him, since they are born of the will of those who sin.
12.1: 12.1 I beseech you. Up to this point he has humbled both sides enough, and nullified glory from the former state; now, as though the business were finished, he proceeds to morality. I beseech you. Up to this point, that neither should be proud against the other; from here, that each should labor for the other's benefit. I beseech by, etc. That is, by the apostleship mercifully committed to me by God, or by the mercy shown and displayed to you by God. A sacrifice, etc. AUG., book 10, On the City of God, ch. 6. A true sacrifice is every work which is done, etc., up to he adds, saying: But be reformed in the newness of your mind, etc.
12.2: 12.2 Be not conformed. A general prohibition. But be reformed. A rule of command. There, continence; here, justice. The former pertains to not coveting, the latter to loving; the former to turning away from evil, the latter to doing good. For by not coveting we are stripped of the old nature, and by loving we are clothed with the new. Be reformed. Because in Adam the image of God was partly lost, so that it begins to be reformed by him by whom it was formed. For it cannot reform itself as it was able to deform itself.
12.3: 12.3 For I say. This is the sacrifice of Christians, that many be one body in Christ. For this is shown to the faithful in the Sacrament of the altar by the wish of the Church, which is signified in the very thing she offers. For as bread is made of many grains, so the holy Church is composed of many members of the faithful, who rejoice together in participation of their Creator; by whose gift they are holy and one, which is also shown in what follows, where he says: We, being many, are one body in Christ I Cor. 10. This cannot be unless they be wise unto sobriety, which is commanded here. To be wise unto sobriety. That is, that it not go beyond the bounds of justice, so that it be useful to us alone and harm no one. The measure of faith. According to the faith which God measuredly distributes; this is faith working through charity, without which no one's works are to be esteemed. To Christ the Spirit was given without measure, but to all the rest he is given, and once given is added to; hence John says of Christ: For God doth not give the Spirit by measure; to the rest it is divided, not indeed the Spirit, but his gifts.
12.4: 12.4 For as in one body. AUG. No one can be just as long as he is separated from the unity of this body, etc., up to but may possess with the piety of using them well.
12.5: 12.5 And everyone members one of another, having, etc. For this, having different goods. Or we are individually members; therefore in the different gifts let this be done; and what those graces are, from whose diversity we are called members, and how in them we ought to serve one another, he opens, saying: Either prophecy, according to the rule of faith, or ministry, etc. Having them, let us be members of others, that we may prophesy for them. Having, I say, according to the rule of faith, because prophecy is given as their faith, or that of the hearers, requires. Note that in the enumeration of graces he begins with prophecy, because the first proof that our faith is reasonable is that believers, having received the Spirit, prophesied.
12.8: 12.8 He that showeth mercy. This mercy is a daily medicine for daily wounds, even if lighter ones; nevertheless judgment without mercy shall be to him that hath not done mercy Jac. 2., and this is surely just, that it be forgiven to the one who forgives and given to the one who gives. But whoever, as though over-just and secure, awaits judgment without mercy, provokes wrath on himself. This mercy is manifold, namely to forgive the sinner, to succor the oppressed, etc.; and therefore he adds about mercy, setting down one member of it when another member has been put first, namely, he that giveth, with simplicity. Simplicity excludes hypocrisy, cheerfulness shows joy, and supported by hope of the future.
12.11: 12.11 Not slothful. Cursed is he who does the work of God negligently; the slothful is without hope in the divine way of life. And therefore, that the chill of sloth may be driven away, Be fervent, etc. Fervent in spirit. THEOD. He called the Spirit grace, etc., up to for he said this. Instant in prayer. That is, doing this assiduously. Serving the Lord, etc. As if he said: Although I have said that you should be fervent in spirit, yet do not thrust the words of God upon people indiscriminately and unseasonably, but be fervent with the opportunity of time, so that you may speak the words of faith in fitting places, to fitting persons and at a fitting time. Fervent. The Spirit is the fire by which charity burns, hence the Lord says: I am come to cast fire on the earth, and what will I, but that it be kindled? Luc. 12.
12.12: 12.12 Rejoicing in hope. Certain of the future, they rejoice, and therefore are patient in tribulation.
12.16: 12.16 Of one mind. Which is not done by the mouth only, for then humility is true if it is not in the tongue alone, lest, presuming on themselves, they do not feel with others in their sorrow, but reproach them.
12.19: 12.19 Give place. He does not command that the saints not wish to be avenged by God, since in the Apocalypse the saints cry out, not indeed to satisfy hatred, but because it is written: The just shall rejoice when he shall see the revenge. But he commands that they, not avenging themselves, give place to the wrath of God who says: Revenge is mine, and I will repay. If therefore the good man wants God to punish his enemy, this is not to render evil for evil. When therefore a just man and a wicked man both want to be avenged by God on their enemies, in what do they differ? The good man desires rather that the enemy be corrected than punished, and when God punishes he does not delight in the enemy's punishment, but is pleased with what pleases the Lord, because he loves him, and it is God whom he follows in this: Who raineth upon the just and the unjust Prov. 25.; and yet even in this world he rebukes the obstinate more harshly and will condemn them at the end, and therefore vengeance is to be reserved for him. He gives place to the wrath of the adversary who permits the adversary to do what he wills.
12.20: 12.20 But if he be hungry. Note the unusual use of but, the conjunction. For it must be read as though neither conjunction were interposed. Or it can also be read so that neither conjunction is superfluous, as if he said: not only do not defend yourselves, but if, etc.
13.1: 13.1 Let every soul. AUG. Exposition of proposition 72 from the Epistle to the Romans. What the Apostle says here most rightly admonishes, etc., up to nevertheless every man should be subject to one above him. For there is no power. Power is from God; but things that are from God are ordered; therefore power is ordered. And so he who resists power resists the ordinance of God; of good power it is clear that God perfected it. Reasonably it may seem so of bad power, since through it the good are purified and the wicked condemned, and it itself is cast down to the worse. And know that by the name of power sometimes is meant the power itself, which is given to someone by God, and sometimes the man himself having power; let the careful reader distinguish this. And those that are, are ordained of God. That is, reasonably arranged by God, hence: God casteth not away the mighty, since he also is mighty Job. 36. GREG. For he desires to imitate God who the height of power, etc., up to because by no means is just power condemned, but the wicked action.
13.2: 13.2 And they that resist. AUG. What if he command what is not lawful? Here, indeed, he will despise the power, fearing a greater power; therefore if the emperor command one thing and God another, setting the former aside God is to be obeyed.
13.3: 13.3 Princes. The Apostle says that those are princes who are appointed for the correction of life and the prohibition of adverse things, having the image of God, so that under one the rest may be. Are not a terror to the good work, etc. If the prince is good, he does not punish one who does well, but loves him. But if he is bad, he does not harm the good man, but purifies him. The wicked subject therefore ought to fear, because princes are instituted to punish evils. Thou shalt have praise from the same. If it is just, from its own praising; if unjust, from its giving you occasion for praise.
13.4: 13.4 For he is God's minister. Rulers have therefore been given so that evils may not be done. An avenger to execute wrath. That is, on account of the wrath of God to be avenged, or an avenger to show forth the wrath of God; because this punishment indicates that those persisting in evil will be punished more severely.
13.6: 13.6 For therefore. You ought to be subject, because for this reason also, that is, to show subjection, you pay tribute, which is a sign of subjection. He does not say, you pay, but you render, as though to those who will give back; because they give back when they fight for the country, and when they conduct judgments, you render, serving God. For by giving them tribute you serve God, because they are ministers of God. Or you render tribute because they are ministers of God, that the good may be praised and the wicked punished.
13.7: 13.7 Tribute. Or tribute, which is paid to lords. Custom duty, which is carried to the lord's house.
13.8: 13.8 Owe no man any thing. Peace to all, love among brothers. For otherwise they are not truly brothers. Love. Mention is made here of charity, because it avails for this humility. For charity alone is that which, even when paid, always keeps the debtor. For it is paid when it is spent, but is owed even if it has been paid, because there is no time when it is not to be spent. Nor is it lost when it is paid, but rather is multiplied by paying; for it is paid by having, not by lacking, unlike money, which cannot be paid unless it is had, nor had unless it is paid; indeed when it is paid by a man, it grows in the man; and the greater it is acquired, the more people it is paid to. He that loveth his neighbor. Though there are two precepts of charity, one is often put for both, because neither is God loved without the neighbor, nor the neighbor without God, nor can he be. Love of neighbor appears in deeds, love of God lies more hidden, and therefore he puts this one more specially, of which the Lord says: A new commandment I give unto you, that you love one another, where that greater commandment of the love of God seems to be passed over. But to those who understand well, both are found in each; because he who loves God cannot despise him whom God commands to be loved, and he who loves his neighbor holily and spiritually, what does he love in him but God? His neighbor, hath fulfilled the law. By neighbor every man must be understood, because there is no one with whom evil is to be done. He who loves men, then, ought to love them either because they are just or so that they may be just. So also he ought to love himself, namely, either because he is just or so that he may be just. For he who loves himself otherwise loves himself unjustly, because he loves himself in order to be unjust, in order therefore to be evil: so now he does not love himself; for he who loveth iniquity hateth his own soul.
13.11: 13.11 And that knowing. Namely that it is the hour, or as some books have: this time, namely of grace, knowing. Now from the time we have had love; it is the hour, that is, the opportunity, but short. To rise from sleep. Sleep is negligence or ignorance. For now. Causes interposed, why we ought to rise. Is nearer. He who does well is close to eternal life. For baptism is for pardon, a good life for the crown. Or nearer, because we are closer to death.
13.12: 13.12 The night is passed. Again it is shown why they ought to rise: because the night of unbelief and ignorance is passed, that is, was; but now it is not, and the memory of it warns you to beware. And the day, that is, eternal beatitude, is at hand, since sins are forgiven, since you are just by grace. The night is the old man, who passed away in baptism; the Day is the sun of justice, Christ, by whose light they have learned the truth, that they may know what is to be done. The works of darkness. Evil works, which came from the darkness of ignorance, or love darkness and lead to darkness
13.13: 13.13 Not in rioting. Note that in these the Romans are touched upon; and therefore they have no right to boast. AUG. Pride is the mother of these diseases, and the greediness of the human mind, which often also begets hypocrisy; this is not resisted unless fear and charity are instilled by frequent testimonies of the divine books.
14.1: 14.1 Now him that is weak. It belongs to perfect faith to distinguish no food, or to think any unclean, because all things are clean to the clean. But some weak ones judged that one should abstain from certain foods, and so there was contention among the Romans; hence he commands that such be taken up, not cast off, but, bearing with them, be raised to faith by example and word. And if it is unknown with what mind someone does it, not to dispute about it. Not in disputations of thoughts. One whose thought is not open is not to be condemned, nor one of whom we do not know what he will be afterward.
14.2: 14.2 The weak. That is the weak man who distinguishes foods, thinking some clean, others unclean, because the Jews were forbidden to eat them; he says this man is to be left to his own judgment, lest he eat with scruple. Or, although faith is perfect, which believes that all things are lawful, yet the weak man, prone to a fall, who is easily laid low by the impulse of lust, may eat herbs, that is, light and dry foods, which are not fuel for vices, and abstain from those by which lust is aroused. For the fatness of meats and delicate feasts provoke the body to lust.
14.3: 14.3 He that eateth. Above he commanded not to dispute about the thoughts of others; here he commands not to despise. Let not judge. AUG., book II, On the Sermon on the Mount. We must judge of what is manifest, not of what is hidden, etc., up to whatever human foods are to be taken indifferently.
14.4: 14.4 To his own lord he standeth. Concerning the unknown heart of another's servant you have no right to judge, but his own Lord, to whose honor he stands who stands; to whom also belongs the fall of the one who falls, who can raise him up or judge him. He standeth or falleth, therefore he says: because it is doubtful, perhaps he stands who is thought to fall. He standeth or falleth. By this he shows that he does not know with what mind that man acts in doubtful matters. And he shall stand. Here he suggests that we ought to turn doubtful things to the better side, and desire the salvation rather than the death of the guilty, and have hope of good in the future, even if it is otherwise in the present. And he shall stand. Because neither if he eats is he guilty, nor if he does not eat, provided he does this out of devotion.
14.5: 14.5 For one man. Above he said that some eat all things, others not all; speaking of kinds of foods he says this, that some abstain at every time, others at a certain time, and he says that both can be rightly done. In his own mind. That is, let him be left to his own judgment, lest, having suffered scandal, he withdraw from charity, which is the mother of all virtues.
14.6: 14.6 He that regardeth. In his own mind I say, as redundant: because he who regardeth the day, either every day or an interposed day, regardeth it to the Lord. And he that eateth, eateth to the Lord. That is, to the honor of the Lord, all of whose creatures he believes clean, and because he is to serve him he is sustained by them.
14.7: 14.7 For none of us liveth to himself. For he who is restrained by law lives not to himself but to God, who gave the law. If there were no law, each would live to himself. To himself. But to the Lord, by whose judgment he is condemned or crowned; or, to himself, that is, to his own praise, but to God's. For as there is no end of his greatness, so there will be no end of our praise. For when we have died in this flesh, we shall not cease to praise God. And according to this he speaks of the faithful only. Or to himself, that is, to be judged by himself, but by the Lord; according to this it is understood of the good and the wicked.
14.10: 14.10 Before the judgment seat. This is said by comparison: for the tribunal is the seat of the judge, which is placed on high so that the judge may be seen by all and himself from the elevated place be able to look upon all. So also Christ will sit as on a tribunal, because he will be seen by all, and himself will see the consciences of all and judge their causes.
14.13: 14.13 Let us not therefore any more. Let us not usurp for ourselves what does not pertain to us. Let us not reprehend things when we do not know with what mind they are done; or even if they are open, let us not so reprehend that we despair of their health. For in these two cases judgment is rash, and proceeds from either pride or lack of evidence, hence it is said: Judge not, and you shall not be judged Luc. 6.
14.14: 14.14 I know and am confident. As if he said, I say: Place no stumblingblock for your brothers. But I do not say stumblingblock or scandal because the food is unclean; because I know this, that my confidence is in Jesus, who, after he came, absolved from the law. He puts common for unclean, drawn from vessels which formerly were common for all uses, some of which afterward, dedicated to sacrifices, were no longer called common but holy; or it is drawn from the Jews, because the Jews themselves were called the proper people of God, but all others common and unclean.
14.16: 14.16 Let not then our good be evil spoken of. Because he who has good works, if he is reproached for some very small thing, his good is obscured, and his good begins to be blasphemed through evil. Hence Ezechiel: The justice of the just shall not avail him, if he has erred Ezech. 33. Let not then our good be evil spoken of. Eating, good in itself, is open to blasphemy when it harms others: and because it harms, abstain, because food is not the cause of the kingdom of God.
14.17: 14.17 For the kingdom of God is not meat and drink. Not the use of foods, but concupiscence is to be restrained. It does not matter what kind of food or how much one takes, according to the suitability of men and one's person and the need of one's health, but how readily and cheerfully he does without them, when it is fitting or necessary to do without them. Joy in the Holy Ghost. For he, etc. Not in feasts, as many are wont, but in the Holy Spirit this joy arises from fraternal peace; as in dispute there is anger, where the Spirit is not, because he is in the peaceful alone; by whose grace also these three are in someone: justice, peace and joy, which were not in these Romans
14.18: 14.18 Pleaseth God, and is approved of men. According as the joy is in the Holy Spirit. And he is held approved by men according to justice, and peace also, because disputation breeds discord, therefore, rash judgments being set aside, let us follow the things that are of peace, not of discord, and of edification, that the others may be edified, or those already edified may be preserved, the Jew with the Gentile, and the Gentile with the Jew.
14.21: 14.21 Is offended. Disturbed, not knowing what to hold. He is offended who departs from right faith.
14.22: 14.22 Blessed. He calls blessed the one who does nothing other than what he approves as useful, but judges that man to be condemned by his own judgment who does not do what he says he ought to do.
14.23: 14.23 And all. Yet not everything that is done with faith is good, because ignorance which is from fault does harm. The whole life of unbelievers is sin, because everyone living or acting unfaithfully sins grievously, and there is nothing good without the highest good, where the knowledge of eternal truth is lacking. Virtue is false even in the best conduct. Works that seem praiseworthy, apart from faith, are like great strength and swift running outside the road. Is not of faith. Our faith requires that a man do what he rightly understands is to be done, and it is sin to do otherwise than he has approved.
15.5: 15.5 To be of one mind. As if he said: Unless you are of one mind, you will not be able to honor God.
15.8: 15.8 Of the circumcision. That is, of the Jews, to whom he came bodily; hence: I was not sent but to the sheep that are lost of the house of Israel Matth. 15. For the truth. He did not reject the Jews, to whom truth belongs properly, and mercy to the Gentiles, to whom no promise had been made. The promises. For he had promised Abraham: In thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed Gen. 22. And David: Of the fruit of thy womb I will set upon thy throne Psalm. 131. And Jacob likewise said: A star shall rise out of Jacob Num. 24.
15.9: 15.9 I will confess. Confession is not only of sins, but also of praise.
15.12: 15.12 There shall be a root of Jesse. And from this root shall be he that shall rise up, etc. Jesse, the root: David, the tree, which through a branch, that is Mary, bore fruit, that is Christ.
15.13: 15.13 And peace. That you may be able to rejoice, may he give peace and concord among one another; and this will be so if the faith is sound. That you may abound. That is, that through these things you may be more certain of eternal beatitude, and abound in the power of the Holy Spirit, that is, in the strength of good working, which is given through the Holy Spirit.
15.14: 15.14 I am certain. Lest the Apostle seem to understand all to be discordant and unwise to be corrected, he removes the reason why he begins, in order to admonish the more perfect about the correction of the lesser; and from this he sets himself forth as an example who labors for others, and it is necessary that these do this, since he himself, hindered by other things, cannot come to them. Filled with all knowledge. By this praise he provokes to better things, in the manner of one exhorting. Hence he does not say to teach, but to admonish; as if to say that it is known but slips from the mind. For this is usually what is admonished, which, though known, sometimes slips from the mind or is held negligently.
15.15: 15.15 Because of the grace. He does not write rashly; but the Apostle of the Gentiles dares to write to all the Gentiles by the authority handed to him through grace.
15.17: 15.17 I have therefore. So you also, if you labor for the brethren. He says this to prove that he is able to do no less than the apostles who had been with Christ.
15.20: 15.20 Not where Christ was named, etc. Because he knew that false apostles and others under the name of Christ were teaching falsehoods, which it would afterward be a task of the greatest labor to correct; therefore he was anxious to forestall them, and to hand on the truth whole, where Christ had not yet been announced; which he proves by the testimony of the prophet.
15.21: 15.21 And they that have not heard, etc. That the understanding of the word of God might be true and inviolable, he hastened to imbue the Gentiles with the truth.
15.26: 15.26 For they have been pleased. He invites the Romans to works of this kind, because he who lives by the mercy of God ought to be dutiful to his fellow brother. The poor. These gave themselves wholly to divine services, caring for nothing worldly, and gave the faithful an example of good conduct.
15.30: 15.30 That you help. Many small ones, when they are gathered in unanimity, become great, and it is impossible that the prayers of many should not obtain. If therefore they desire to see him, let them pray that they may receive him delivered with the joy of charity; hence follows that I may be delivered.
15.31: 15.31 Acceptable. That they, understanding his charity toward them, may give thanks to God in unanimity with him. For it is a great advantage to him, by whose ministry many, made glad, praise God.
15.33: 15.33 And the God of peace. Christ, who said: My peace I give to you, and my peace I leave to you Joan. 14.; who is with his own until the consummation of the world, so may he be with you; for it is he who says: Behold I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the world Matth. 28.
16.1: 16.1 And I commend to you. From here the Apostle sets forth many just persons, whom Rome ought to believe, as if to say: Do as I have said, and imitate these. Phebe. Namely Phebe was a very rich and very noble woman, who supported the Church in the place called Cenchrae with her substance. At that time she had set out for Rome on some business, and by her perhaps he sent this Epistle.
16.2: 16.2 That you receive her worthily. Or, as other codices have, very honorably and with honor.
16.3: 16.3 Prisca and Aquila. Aquila is the husband of Priscilla: these helpers of Paul had come to Rome for the confirmation of the Romans. So also all the others whom he greets are understood to have been at Rome.
16.4: 16.4 Of the Gentiles. Because these labor for the progress of the Gentiles, exhorting to the faith of Christ, and did not refuse to suffer dangers for the Apostle; hence the Romans also ought to obey them.
16.10: 16.10 Apelles. Through temptations he was found faithful in Christ: though not his own friend, or a sharer in the work.
16.11: 16.11 Aristobulus. This Aristobulus used to gather the brethren in Christ, whom the Apostle greets, thereby approving his deed. Of Narcissus. Narcissus is said to have been a presbyter, as is read in other codices, who by traveling confirmed the holy brethren; since he was not present then, he greets his own; and because he did not know the merits of all of them, he distinguishes, adding: who are in the Lord, that is, those whom you know to be worthy.
16.12: 16.12 Hath labored. The labor here, of which the Apostle speaks rather often, is in exhortation and in the ministry of the saints, and in pressure and in want for God's sake.
16.13: 16.13 And mine. For his holiness he calls her his mother, whose son he preferred for ecclesiastical office.
16.15: 16.15 And all. He bids all to whom he writes and whom he names to greet one another with a holy kiss, that is, in the peace of Christ, so that the kisses may be religious, not carnal.
16.16: 16.16 Of Christ. That is, those which trust in Christ, not in anything else.
16.17: 16.17 That you mark. He touches on the false apostles, whom he warns are to be avoided throughout the whole Epistle.
16.19: 16.19 For your. Therefore I admonish you to avoid them, because your faith and obedience are praised everywhere: because you are at the head of the world, and so by your example others could now be corrupted. Or, I ask you to avoid them, because you have obeyed lightly, which is good, and I rejoice at it; but I want you to be wise in discerning good, and without any part of evil.
16.20: 16.20 And the God. May you be wise: and may God crush Satan, that is, false preachers, or any man opposing you, or the devil. Under your feet. That you may despise the head, that is, the first motions of suggestions, and if it is the devil, may crush his head, as was said to Eve in figure of the Church, or of sensuality. The grace. The grace which he promised at his coming, he already wishes for them.
16.21: 16.21 Timothy saluteth you. As if he said: So many and so great rejoice together at your beginning, and therefore it is fitting that you persevere.
16.23: 16.23 And the whole. Above he had said all the Churches; but here he says the Church of another province, from which Caius was.
16.25: 16.25 Now to him. So I admonish you. Now to him who is able to establish you, be glory, from whom alone, who is good, all goods are; in which the sum of the epistle is noted, because here the Apostle principally intends to admonish them to attribute all things to the grace of God. According to the revelation. He calls the mystery the incarnation of Christ, etc., which was hidden in eternal times: because although it was known in some part to the ancient fathers, yet it was fully known by none, until in its own time it was revealed through Christ himself.
16.26: 16.26 By the scriptures of the prophets. Unlocked by him, giving testimony to this preaching. Made known to all nations for the obedience, that is, that they may obey the faith by working well. Kept silent to others, but known to God alone: because although it is now revealed to men, yet it is known to God alone, because he alone knows why it was so done. In this he restrains the inquirers who ask why God delayed so long? why he permitted so many nations to perish.
16.27: 16.27 To whom be honor. AUG. As for what is added: To whom be glory, etc., up to because through him God the Trinity was made known to men, which is the mystery.
